fields.reasoningExclude: Hide the reasoning from the response

constraints.reasoningTemp: Reasoning models use a fixed temperature of 1.0. This parameter will be ignored by the API.
constraints.reasoningSingleLevel: This model accepts a single reasoning depth.
constraints.reasoningBudgetRange: Between {{min}} and {{max}} tokens. Leave empty to let the depth decide.

tooltips.temperature: Controls randomness in responses. Low (0-0.3): precise, deterministic outputs. High (0.7-1.0): more creative and varied responses.
tooltips.topP: Alternative to temperature. Only considers tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds this threshold. 0.1 = very focused, 1.0 = full vocabulary.
tooltips.frequencyPenalty: Reduces repetition by penalizing tokens already frequent in the output. Positive (0.5-1.0) discourages verbatim repetition. Range: -2 to 2.
tooltips.presencePenalty: Encourages topic diversity. Penalizes each token that has appeared, regardless of frequency. Positive = explores more topics. Range: -2 to 2.
tooltips.maxTokens: Maximum number of output tokens. Limits the length of the generated response. Optimal value depends on the agent type.
tooltips.timeout: Maximum wait time in seconds before aborting the API call. Leave empty to use the provider's default.
tooltips.reasoningEffort: Controls the model's internal thinking intensity. Higher = better accuracy but increased latency and cost. Lower = fast responses for simple tasks.

config.thinkingBudgetBelowFloor: Reasoning is enabled, but the effective max tokens ({{maxTokens}}) is below the safety floor of {{floor}}. Reasoning consumes the response budget, so replies would come back truncated or empty. Raise max tokens to at least {{floor}}, or turn reasoning off. Note: leaving max tokens empty inherits the code default.

skills.title: LIA Capabilities (skills)
skills.description: Skills extend the assistant's capabilities with expert instructions and specialized workflows.
skills.empty: No imported skills. Import SKILL.md files to add new capabilities.
skills.admin_description: Skills shipped with the application. Read-only.
skills.desc_briefing-quotidien: Generates a comprehensive morning briefing combining calendar events, priority tasks, and weather forecast. Use when the user asks for a daily briefing or morning summary.
skills.desc_redaction-professionnelle: Provides expert guidance for writing professional emails, reports, and messages with appropriate tone, structure, and formulas. Use for formal communications or business correspondence.
skills.desc_synthese-recherche: Guides structured web research with source cross-referencing and critical synthesis. Use when the user needs in-depth research or comprehensive analysis of a topic.
skills.desc_preparation-reunion: Prepares meeting materials by gathering calendar details, participant contacts, and recent email history. Use when the user mentions preparing for a meeting.
skills.desc_coaching-productivite: Provides productivity coaching with prioritization frameworks (Eisenhower, Pomodoro) and habit-building strategies. Use when the user asks for help organizing tasks or managing time.
skills.guide_format: .md file: a single SKILL.md file with a YAML header (name, description) followed by Markdown instructions.
skills.guide_zip: .zip file: a compressed folder containing SKILL.md and optionally sub-folders (references/, scripts/, assets/).
skills.guide_frontmatter: The YAML header must start with --- and contain at least the name and description fields.
skills.guide_marketplace: Compatible with agentskills.io standard skills (skillsmp.com, GitHub, etc.).
skills.translate_button_label: Translate description of {{name}} to all languages
skills.delete_admin_confirm_description: Skill "{{name}}" will be permanently deleted from the system. This action cannot be undone.
skills.edit_description_hint: Write the description in your language. It will be automatically translated to English (stored in SKILL.md) and all 6 interface languages.
skills.guide_modal_subtitle: Learn how to create skills to customize and extend LIA's capabilities.
skills.guide_modal_what_body: A skill is a SKILL.md file that gives the assistant expert instructions for a specific domain. The assistant reads these instructions and applies them automatically when relevant — without you having to repeat the context each time. Skills can include reference documents, Python scripts, and templates.
skills.guide_archetype_prompt_expert_desc: Expert instructions the assistant follows for a domain (coaching, writing, methodology…). No specific tools — the assistant applies its conversational expertise.
skills.guide_archetype_advisory_desc: A structured methodology where the assistant uses available tools organically (calendar, emails, contacts…). It decides which tools to call based on context.
skills.guide_archetype_plan_template_desc: A deterministic workflow with predefined tool calls, executed in sequence or in parallel. Ideal for recurring routines (briefings, reports, audits…).
skills.guide_activation_body: Skills use a 3-tier loading model to optimize token consumption:
skills.guide_tier_l1: Catalogue — Name and description loaded at session start (~50 tokens/skill)
skills.guide_tier_l2: Instructions — Full SKILL.md body loaded when the skill is activated (< 5000 tokens)
skills.guide_tier_l3: Resources — Individual files (references/, scripts/, assets/) loaded on demand
skills.guide_modal_tip_1: Write the description in English, third person: "Generates...", "Provides...", "Guides..."
skills.guide_modal_tip_2: The description should state what the skill does AND when to use it (the trigger).
skills.guide_modal_tip_3: Keep instructions concise and structured — prefer numbered lists.
skills.guide_modal_tip_4: Name your skill in kebab-case: my-skill (lowercase, hyphens, no spaces).
skills.guide_modal_tip_5: List available resources at the end of SKILL.md with their relative path and a description.
skills.guide_modal_tip_6: Test with simple queries before making the skill more complex.
skills.guide_modal_format_intro: A SKILL.md file starts with a YAML header (between ---) containing metadata, followed by a Markdown body with the detailed instructions.
skills.guide_field_category: UI grouping (quotidien, recherche, communication, organisation, productivite, developpement)
skills.guide_field_always_loaded: Always inject instructions (costs tokens every conversation)
skills.guide_field_outputs: Declared output channels (text, frame, image) — only for Visualizer / Generator skills
skills.guide_field_compatibility: Prerequisites shown in the catalogue (e.g. "Requires Calendar connector")
skills.guide_runtime_intro: When your skill uses a Python script, the LIA platform auto-provides several behaviors — here is what to know to produce skills that blend in naturally.
skills.guide_runtime_autoparams_body: Every run_skill_script call receives the user's language (_lang) and timezone (_tz) in its parameters. Use _lang to localize your labels via inline translation tables.
skills.guide_runtime_autoparams_hint: Do not rely on locale.setlocale — slim container images don't ship system locales, so strftime silently falls back to English.
skills.guide_runtime_theme_body: Use html[data-theme="dark"] CSS selectors rather than @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark). A runtime snippet injected by LIA applies the data-theme attribute and the lang on <html>, kept in sync with the app.
skills.guide_runtime_resize_body: Iframes self-resize to match the content height. The aspect_ratio you declare is only the initial skeleton before measurement. Keep html/body margins default, style your own inner containers.
skills.guide_runtime_example_qr: Generator example (QR code via segno, localized caption):
skills.guide_runtime_interactive_note: Recommended pattern for any interactive frame: client JS with crypto.getRandomValues and addEventListener — inline onclick is blocked by CSP on user skills.
skills.guide_example_simple_desc: The simplest type — pure instructions the assistant follows when the topic comes up. No tools or plan needed.
skills.guide_example_advisory_desc: The assistant follows a methodology and uses available tools (calendar, emails, contacts) organically as needed.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_intro: Skills can emit interactive iframes and generated images by writing a JSON object on stdout. The skill decides what to render — all three channels (text, frame, image) are independent and can coexist.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_text_label: Always required — caption used for voice, LLM context, and accessibility.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_frame_label: Optional interactive iframe (inline HTML via srcDoc or external HTTPS URL).
skills.guide_rich_outputs_image_label: Optional image artifact (data: URI or HTTPS URL) with required alt text.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_example_map: Visualizer example — interactive Google Maps embed:
skills.guide_rich_outputs_example_qr: Generator example — QR code image generated from text:
skills.guide_rich_outputs_sandbox: All frames render inside an iframe sandbox without allow-same-origin — parent cookies and storage are unreachable regardless of the frame content.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_csp: When a user-owned skill emits frame.html, LIA automatically injects a strict Content Security Policy that blocks outbound fetch/XHR (connect-src none) and nested iframes (frame-src none). System skills are trusted and skip CSP injection.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_csp_warning: Consequence: user-skill inline frames cannot call external APIs. For external data, use frame.url instead (the remote site controls its own headers).
skills.guide_rich_outputs_tip_1: Write only the JSON on stdout — put logs and progress on stderr.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_tip_2: frame.html and frame.url are mutually exclusive — a frame has one source.
skills.guide_rich_outputs_tip_3: Always set image.alt for accessibility and voice fallback.
skills.guide_modal_struct_body: For complex skills, import a .zip file containing SKILL.md and optional sub-folders:
skills.guide_struct_scripts: Python scripts executed in a sandbox
skills.guide_resource_references_desc: Text documents (.md, .txt) the assistant can read on demand via read_skill_resource. Ideal for storing detailed guides, templates, or reference data too large for the SKILL.md.
skills.guide_resource_references_usage: Usage: mention the file in the "Available Resources" section of your SKILL.md — the assistant will read them automatically.
skills.guide_resource_scripts_desc: Python scripts (.py) executed in an isolated sandbox via run_skill_script. They receive data as JSON on stdin and return results as JSON on stdout.
skills.guide_resource_scripts_usage: Usage: describe the script and its parameters in SKILL.md. The assistant will execute it when needed.
skills.guide_resource_assets_desc: Static files (images, HTML/CSV templates, JSON data) accessible for reading. Useful for output templates, logos, or configurations.
skills.guide_resource_assets_usage: Usage: reference them in the instructions. The assistant can read and use them to format responses.
skills.guide_import_body: Import a single SKILL.md file for a simple skill, or a .zip file containing the complete folder (SKILL.md + references/ + scripts/ + assets/). Use the "Import" button above. Limits: 100 KB for SKILL.md, 50 KB per resource file, 20 skills max per user.
skills.guide_modal_plan_body: The plan_template defines a sequence of tools executed automatically, bypassing the LLM planner. Ideal for recurring, predictable workflows. Steps without depends_on run in parallel.
skills.guide_modal_plan_field_agent_name: Agent name, required for a TOOL step (see catalogue below)
skills.guide_modal_plan_field_tool_name: Tool name to call, required for a TOOL step
skills.guide_modal_plan_field_step_type: Type: TOOL (default), CONDITIONAL, REPLAN or HUMAN
skills.guide_autotrigger_body: Skills with plan_template are auto-triggered when the user's query covers ALL domains in the template. E.g., a skill with event_agent + weather_agent triggers when the user asks for both their schedule and the weather.
skills.guide_tools_intro: Complete reference of agents and their tools with parameters and types. Use exact names in the plan_template's agent_name and tool_name. Parameters marked * are required.
skills.guide_tools_note: Tools marked "Connector" work with Google, Microsoft, or Apple depending on the connected provider. MCP agents (external servers) are dynamic and cannot be used in static plan_templates.
skills.param_content_instruction: AI instruction to compose the body
skills.param_color: Color (red, blue, warm_white… or CIE x,y)
skills.param_source_image: UUID of the source image to edit
skills.guide_scripts_body: Skills can include Python scripts executed in an isolated sandbox. Scripts receive data via stdin (JSON) and return results via stdout (JSON). Useful for calculations, data transformations, or custom processing.
skills.guide_scripts_rule_1: Only .py files in the scripts/ folder are allowed
skills.guide_scripts_rule_2: Scripts run in a sandbox with a limited timeout
skills.guide_scripts_rule_3: Communication via stdin/stdout in JSON format
skills.guide_skill_tools_body: The assistant has 3 special tools to interact with activated skills. These tools are called automatically — you don't need to reference them in your instructions.
skills.guide_skilltool_activate: Loads the full instructions (L2) of a skill
skills.guide_skilltool_read: Reads a reference or asset file from the skill
skills.guide_skilltool_run: Executes a Python script from the scripts/ folder
skills.guide_modal_compat_body: Skills are 100% compatible with the agentskills.io ecosystem — the same format is used by Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, GitHub Copilot and 30+ other products. Import skills from marketplaces like skillsmp.com.
skills.guide_modal_link: Learn more about the agentskills.io standard

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Find answers to the most common questions about LIA

intro.title: How LIA Works
intro.description: A multi-agent AI assistant that connects your services and answers with your own data.

architecture.title: 🏗️ LangGraph Multi-Agent Architecture
architecture.description: LIA runs on LangGraph, a state graph: 20+ specialised agents (email, calendar, contacts, files, weather, web, home…) plus MCP agents added at runtime, each with conditional transitions and state checkpointed to PostgreSQL — so a conversation survives a restart in the middle of a task.

queryAnalyzer.title: 🧭 Query Analyzer v3.2
queryAnalyzer.description: One LLM pass (P95 under 800 ms) reads the request: action or conversation, which domains it touches and with what confidence, which references need resolving — and the risks it carries, such as a mutation, an unbounded volume, or a per-item loop. Related domains are pulled in from the type registry.

routing.title: 🧭 Semantic Routing & AI-Powered Embeddings
routing.description: The router reads meaning, not keywords: multilingual embeddings across 100+ languages, related domains pulled in automatically (weather → location, calendar → contacts), and a capabilities catalogue filtered down to what the request actually needs — 96 % fewer tokens than handing over everything.

query.title: 🔍 Query Analysis
query.description: Intent, named entities, time and place constraints, action type (read, create, modify, delete). When the request stays ambiguous, LIA asks a clarifying question instead of guessing.

planning.title: 📋 Intelligent Planning & FOR_EACH
planning.description: The planner writes the plan before acting: parallel steps with dependencies, a FOR_EACH pattern for bulk work (“email everyone in this group”), and around 100 pre-trained patterns so common requests are planned right the first time. The catalogue it reads is closed and honest — every tool needed to obtain a datum is present, and every limit the validator enforces is published, so a plan is never failed for obeying instructions it was never given.

semanticTypes.title: 📦 Semantic Type System
semanticTypes.description: 100 semantic types in a DAG hierarchy (inspired by schema.org and RDF) link every tool to the data it consumes and produces, from a live source: the annotations the tools themselves carry, MCP tools included. That is what lets a chain cross domains, blocks a person's name where an address is expected, and pulls in the tool able to supply a missing datum.

semanticValidation.title: ✅ Semantic Plan Validation
semanticValidation.description: Before execution, an LLM looks for 15 classes of anomaly — hallucinated capability, ghost dependency, logical cycle, cardinality mismatch, temporal paradox… — and rates how reversible the action is. The verdict classifies, it does not convict: a flagged plan still runs, and usually succeeds. A capability is called blocked only when it produced nothing, and when automatic repairs run out the user gets a question in their own language, never the internal diagnosis.

semantic.title: 🎯 Semantic Validation & Pivot
semantic.description: Plans are checked for logical inconsistency before they run, and a query that failed is reformulated automatically — synonyms, broader criteria, decomposition — instead of being handed back as a dead end.

context.title: 🧠 Advanced Context Management
context.description: “The first email”, “send him a message”: an entity-resolution engine keeps a typed registry of what the conversation produced — emails, contacts, events — and asks you when two candidates are equally likely. It quotes the time it read, never the one it remembers, and says plainly when something was never retrieved.

memory.title: 💾 Dual Short/Long-Term Memory
memory.description: Short term: a sliding message window, summarised automatically, with the token-to-threshold ratio always visible in the chat header. Long term: facts about you — preferences, relationships, habits — found by comparing your question both to a memory's content and to its trigger words, keeping whichever matches better. Standing rules count too: tell LIA once how to work for you and it applies every time. When a fact changes, the old one is superseded with a date rather than erased.

interests.title: ✨ Smart Interest Learning
interests.description: Interests are learned from conversation — but asking about a subject is a task, not a taste. A new interest needs one of four named grounds: a stated passion, your own practice, prior knowledge, or digging into the same subject across an exchange — and the model must quote the words that carry it. Selection then draws with two-level rarity, so one passion never monopolises what you are shown.

habits.title: 🧭 Habit Learning
habits.description: LIA learns your rhythm — active hours, weekday against weekend, recurring requests — with calibrated statistics rather than an opaque model, and publishes all of it: the thresholds applied, the days observed, the progress left. Off by default, and when nothing is detected it tells you the exact bar that was not met.

summarization.title: 📝 Automatic Summarization
summarization.description: Long conversations are summarised as they go, so the context keeps its thread without hitting the token ceiling: key facts extracted, the rest compressed, the summary injected back into the prompt.

hitl.title: 👤 Advanced Human-in-the-Loop
hitl.description: Eight moments where LIA hands the decision back: clarification, disambiguation, plan approval, tool confirmation, draft critique, edit confirmation, bulk confirmation, and validation of a mass deletion. Whether an action counts as a mutation is read from the tool's declared category, never guessed from its name — so a bulk reply is gated exactly like a deletion. And a confirmation is never asked twice: a question you have to answer again is not extra safety, it is being made to insist in order to be obeyed.

connectors.title: 🔌 Connectors & Registry
connectors.description: One modular registry for every service — Google (Gmail, Calendar, Contacts, Tasks, Drive, Places, Routes), Apple iCloud, Microsoft 365, OpenWeatherMap, Wikipedia, Perplexity, Brave. Each connector declares its own manifest, its JSON schemas are generated from the Python types, and OAuth, API keys and credentials are handled the same way for all of them.

streaming.title: ⚡ Streaming & Real-Time
streaming.description: The answer streams over SSE with typed events: each execution step appears live — routing, planning, validation, tool calls — then the text arrives token by token. A stream that goes quiet no longer freezes the interface: when a phone suspends the tab the connection dies without saying so, so past a silence budget the client drops it and reattaches to the turn still running, which replays what was produced meanwhile.

richResponses.title: 🎨 Rich Answers & Display Modes
richResponses.description: Three rendering modes, yours to pick: HTML cards per domain, rich HTML, or Markdown. Rich HTML lays out answers with seven design-system components — callouts, icon badges, collapsible sections, key-value lists, columns, numbered steps, stat tiles — under a restraint rule of two or three per answer. Highlighted code with a copy button, LaTeX, zebra tables; every tag crosses a strict sanitisation boundary, and copying always yields clean text.

llm.title: 🤖 Multi-Provider LLM & Pattern Learning
llm.description: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Perplexity and local Ollama, each behind its own adapter: reasoning budget, token counting and structured-output format are translated per provider, never guessed. Bayesian learning of planning patterns bypasses the LLM above 90 % confidence — 89 % fewer tokens on average — and a budget floor refuses at boot any configuration where reasoning would eat the answer.

security.title: 🔐 Multi-Layer Security
security.description: Defence in depth, from sign-in to storage: passkeys, TOTP with backup codes, step-up re-authentication for sensitive actions, and every active session visible and revocable. Underneath, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, PII filtered out of the logs, isolation between users, encryption at rest, a GDPR export where secret material is unexportable by construction, and daily backups whose restore is tested. A skill runs in a throwaway container with no socket and no network. And any text written by a third party — email, invitation, web page, MCP server — reaches the model tagged as data to analyse, never as instruction.

resilience.title: 🛡️ Performance & Token Optimization
resilience.description: Text compaction cuts about 97 % per entity, message windowing another 93 %. Circuit breakers guard external APIs, a multi-level Redis cache absorbs the repeats, OAuth tokens refresh in the background before they expire, and rate limiting is distributed with exponential retry. Background jobs start at staggered times rather than together, because periods that share a divisor align forever — and calls to the embedding provider wait briefly for a slot instead of being refused, a wait that always expires open.

voice.title: 🎙️ Full Voice Mode
voice.description: Speak and be spoken to. Speech recognition defaults to free, on-server Whisper (99+ languages, audio never leaves the server); each user can opt into remote ElevenLabs Scribe for higher accuracy on conversational speech. Three voice providers are seeded, with sentence-level streaming so the first audio starts in about a second. Paid calls carry a per-message cost badge, and a duration cap protects against spikes. Wake word or microphone button, automatic end-of-speech detection — and the spoken text is stripped of markup so the voice reads the sentence, nothing else.

reminders.title: 🔔 Reminders & Push Notifications
reminders.description: Reminders created in plain language, pushed to every device, with timezones converted for you and references resolved (“the next one”, a number, a piece of content). Each message is written with the active personality and your memories, in your own language. Due reminders are taken under lease before delivery, and every early exit releases it — so an undelivered reminder comes back on the next pass instead of vanishing.

personalities.title: 🎭 14 Dynamic Personalities
personalities.description: Fourteen personalities to pick from (Normal, Enthusiastic, Professor, Friend, Influencer, Philosopher, Cynic, Poet, Coach…), each defining tone, style and behaviour, with prompts written in all six languages. Administrators can create, edit and disable them; each user picks their own.

geolocation.title: 📍 Smart Geolocation
geolocation.description: Three sources, one cascade: your live browser position, otherwise the last remembered one (opt-in, encrypted, never historised, under 24 h old), otherwise your configured home address. Chat, scheduled actions, briefing and skills all read the same rule — and a remembered position always travels with its age (“based on your last known position at 9:30”), never dressed up as current. “At home” is never resolved from a position captured on the road.

i18n.title: 🌍 Complete Internationalization
i18n.description: Six languages end to end (EN, FR, DE, ES, IT, ZH): interface, localised dates, agent answers in your language, browser detection. Key parity across the six files is checked on every commit — a missing translation blocks the release instead of printing a raw key on screen. Search goes further than literal translation: every setting carries synonyms written language by language, and case, accents and curly apostrophes are ignored, so an ordinary keyboard reaches every screen.

observability.title: 📊 Production-Ready Observability
observability.description: The full stack: Prometheus metrics (tokens, latency, errors, cost), 26 Grafana dashboards, Tempo tracing, Loki logs, and email alerting where every alert links its runbook. The 26th dashboard is a product cockpit counting validated outcomes — your explicit 👍, or an action left uncorrected for a full day — and derives activation, retention and cost per useful result from them. The counting lives in PostgreSQL, and Grafana reads it through a role that can only see aggregates.

tools.title: 🔧 90 Typed Tools
tools.description: 90 native tools with JSON schemas generated from the Python types, extended without limit by MCP servers and skills. Each declares its manifest and its published bounds: whatever a validator can reject, the planner can read. The catalogue is filtered per domain — which is why every domain carries its read capabilities too, or a domain holding only write tools would push the planner to write.

costTransparency.title: 💰 Cost Transparency
costTransparency.description: Optional live display: input, output and cache tokens, cost in euros per message and for the conversation, plus cycle statistics. A quota no longer arrives as a wall: a warning appears at 80 % of whichever limit binds first — tokens, messages or cost — naming it and giving the reset date, or stating that an absolute limit never resets. A ceiling may also cover the whole instance, and LIA says so rather than blaming your personal quota. The counting is a contract: a paid call that would complete without a count raises an alert, and each call is valued at the tariff of its exact moment.

scheduledActions.title: 📅 Scheduled Actions
scheduledActions.description: Recurring actions the assistant runs on its own: pick the days and the time, attach an instruction, and LIA executes it. Results are archived in the conversation and pushed to you, with auto-disable after five consecutive failures. The notification carries the same final text that was archived, flattened to plain text before truncation.

mcp.title: 🔌 MCP (Model Context Protocol)
mcp.description: Full MCP support, with admin-wide and per-user servers, speaking both protocol generations — the new stateless revision and the legacy handshake, with automatic fallback. Four authentication types (none, API key, bearer token, OAuth 2.1 with issuer-bound credentials), automatic tool discovery, and generated domain descriptions so the router knows what each server is for.

mcpApps.title: 📱 Interactive MCP Apps
mcpApps.description: Interactive HTML widgets rendered inside the conversation, in a sandboxed iframe with a JSON-RPC bridge over PostMessage for forms, downloads and links. The sandbox runs without allow-same-origin, origins are validated, and COEP credentialless lets external fonts and modules load without weakening the isolation. Available to administrators and users alike.

excalidraw.title: 🎨 Excalidraw Generation
excalidraw.description: Diagrams generated in two stages: the planner writes a high-level intent — components, connections, layout — and dedicated LLM calls then produce every Excalidraw shape and arrow. Architecture diagrams, workflows, org charts and more, with a format cheat sheet injected for accuracy and its own configurable model.

multichannel.title: 📲 Multi-Channel (Telegram)
multichannel.description: A generic multi-channel architecture, with Telegram as the first implementation: OTP binding, text and voice (audio messages transcribed), and an asynchronous webhook that claims each update once so a redelivery is never replayed. An external channel is not a degraded mode — long-term memory, journals and emotional state apply there identically, and a single preference resolution serves both incoming messages and button replies, precisely so none can be forgotten on one side only.

heartbeatAutonome.title: 💓 Autonomous Heartbeat
heartbeatAutonome.description: Proactive notifications built from eleven data sources aggregated live, in two phases: a cheap model decides whether to speak at all, then the message is rewritten in the active personality. Topics rotate through a varied interest sample with an anti-repetition window, so the same theme never returns day after day, and a notification about an interest fetches real facts with clickable sources. One switch per source — being connected to a service and being interrupted by it are two separate decisions — and a source that drops out is counted and timed rather than silently missing.

webFetch.title: 🌐 Intelligent Web Fetch
webFetch.description: Fetch and read any public URL, no API key needed: readability extraction turns an article, a documentation page or a dataset into clean Markdown, straight into the conversation. Multi-layer SSRF protection — DNS validation, post-redirect re-checking, size limits, per-user rate limiting.

knowledgeEnrichment.title: 📰 Brave Search Contextual Enrichment
knowledgeEnrichment.description: Before answering, LIA can look things up with Brave Search (web and news) to contextualise what it knows: news, prices, opening hours, an event under way. Smart Redis caching keeps the API calls down, and each user brings their own Brave key from Settings › Connectors.

adaptiveReplanner.title: 🔄 Adaptive Replanning
adaptiveReplanner.description: Execution failures are analysed by rules, with no extra LLM call: empty result, partial failure, broken dependency or reference. The analysis classifies what happened and computes a recovery decision — retry, re-plan, ask, abort — which is advisory today: logged and counted so the failure modes are measurable. Partial results are surfaced rather than discarded, and a failure a retry cannot change is no longer called transient.

semanticLeakDefense.title: 🛡️ Indexable vs Semantic criteria distinction
semanticLeakDefense.description: A universal layer separating what a tool can really filter — a date, an identifier, a sender, a status — from what only a model can judge: category, urgency, quality. When the planner tries to search a literal-search tool for a conceptual word like “medical” or “urgent”, the leak is detected and counted. No connector or future MCP server needs changing: a manifest can opt out declaratively, and the operator picks observe, autocorrect or off.

parallelExecution.title: ⚡ Wave-by-Wave Parallel Execution
parallelExecution.description: A native parallel engine built on asyncio: the dependency graph is turned into execution waves, so independent steps run at the same time and dependent ones wait for their prerequisites. A multi-domain plan — weather, routes, places and calendar — finishes in seconds instead of one step after another.

dataRegistry.title: 🗂️ Data Registry & Rich Rendering
dataRegistry.description: A unified structured-data layer behind the rich cards: 24 registry types (contact, email, event, task, file, place, route, weather, MCP app…), immutable items with metadata, TTL and deterministic ids, sent over SSE before the text so the cards render instantly. Related results are correlated automatically — an event and its route travel together — and every type carries its provenance: produced by LIA, or written by a third party and flagged as such to the model.

qualityAssurance.title: 🎯 LLM-as-Judge Quality Assurance
qualityAssurance.description: An automated evaluation pipeline scores answers on three axes — relevance to the question, fabricated content, and latency against its SLA — and exports the metrics to Prometheus and Langfuse, so a quality drift is seen rather than reported. On the test side, a static guard refuses to let a module disable itself when a provider key is missing: a skipped test is green, therefore invisible — ten files had hidden 219 tests that had never run once.

attachments.title: 📎 Photos & File Attachments
attachments.description: Photos and PDFs added through the 📎 button, drag and drop, or a straight Ctrl+V from the clipboard, compressed in the browser before they leave. Images are read by a configurable vision model, PDFs have their text extracted, and thumbnails appear inline with an accessible lightbox. Strict per-user isolation and automatic cleanup — on conversation reset, and after 24 hours.

skills.title: Skills (with interactive maps & mini-apps)
skills.description: Give LIA expert skills of your own. Write one in plain language with the built-in generator — installed instantly — or import from agentskills.io-compatible marketplaces. A skill can return an interactive HTML frame (map, dashboard, converter) or an image alongside its text, with theme and locale synced automatically, and the gallery shows what each one actually produces rather than a generic icon. Ask LIA to adjust a skill and it re-reads the whole package, then shows you what will be replaced and what will disappear before writing anything.

ragSpaces.title: 📚 RAG Knowledge Spaces
ragSpaces.description: Create knowledge spaces and upload your own documents (PDF, TXT, MD, DOCX): text is extracted, chunked and embedded, and an active space enriches the answers through a hybrid search that combines semantic similarity with keyword matching. Costs are tracked per document and per query. The built-in corpus that lets LIA answer about itself is rebuilt by one process at a time and checked at every start against both the source files and what is stored — and embeddings are computed before anything is deleted, so a provider rejection costs nothing and the previous corpus keeps answering.

subAgents.title: Sub-Agents
subAgents.description: Complex work is delegated to ephemeral specialists running in parallel, whose results the assistant orchestrates and synthesises for you. Each sub-agent runs a bounded loop — ten iterations at most — over an explicitly allowlisted toolset rather than the whole catalogue, because a delegation that explores never converges. Its instruction is capped in tokens with its own timeout and ceiling, so a longer reasoning budget never requires raising the application-wide limit.

browserControl.title: 🌐 Browser Control
browserControl.description: Autonomous browsing for what an API cannot reach: searching an e-commerce site, filling a form, extracting data from a JavaScript-rendered page. The agent drives the site's own controls — search boxes, autocomplete, forms — re-checks the page after each action, and on a transactional flow stops at the login or payment step and reports back. It never enters credentials and never submits a payment.

psycheEngine.title: 🧠 Psyche Engine
psycheEngine.description: A psychological state that moves with every exchange: 14 moods, 22 emotions, energy, the relationship with you, personality traits. The assistant adapts its tone, its vocabulary and its behaviour organically — it never announces it, it shows it — and the mood avatar animates on the current reply. Built-in emotional safety: memories with a strong negative charge trigger a protective mode.

personalJournals.title: 📓 Personal Journals (stratified consciousness)
personalJournals.description: LIA keeps journals of its own, on four levels — raw observation, operational directive, transversal pattern, portrait facet — each with a confidence and its evidence and contradiction counters. A deferred loop re-evaluates at the next turn whether an injected directive was confirmed or contradicted by you, at no added LLM cost, and the same pass compiles the user portrait that reaches the eight flows where LIA speaks. You keep control: read by theme or level, edit, flag a problem, trigger a consolidation. Counters are incremented by the system, never by the model, and no directive reaches high confidence without real evidence.

healthMetrics.title: 🩺 iPhone health data (polymorphic batch upsert)
healthMetrics.description: Steps and heart rate sent from your iPhone shortcuts to a token-authenticated endpoint — the token is stored hashed and shown to you once. Samples carry their own timestamps, are normalised to UTC, deduplicated within a batch with the right arbitration per kind (the maximum for steps, the average for heart rate, so overlapping Watch and phone samples do not collide), and an out-of-range sample is rejected individually with its reason rather than sinking the batch. Gaps are preserved so the charts stay honest.

imageGeneration.title: 🎨 Image Generation & Editing
imageGeneration.description: Generate images from a description, or edit an existing one with plain-language instructions, across several providers with your own quality, size and format preferences and per-image cost tracking. A generated image is an attachment with a limited life: the card shows the deadline the server returned — never a duration hard-coded in the interface — and turns to an alert tone in the final hours, so downloading stays possible. The time allowed follows the model's real duration, measured per quality and format, so a detailed image is not cut off just before the end.

documentGeneration.title: Document Generation
documentGeneration.description: LIA writes complete, downloadable documents on demand: CSV and Excel spreadsheets, Word reports, PowerPoint decks with speaker notes, PDF, Markdown, plain text. A dedicated writer model produces the content in your language — grounded in the data you provided or in research done in the same request — then a local renderer builds the exact file, with no third-party document service involved. Files appear as cards under the answer with their name, size and expiry, and everything is temporary by design: download what you want to keep.

reactMode.title: ⚡ ReAct Execution Mode
reactMode.description: The alternative to the pipeline: the assistant reasons step by step — calling a tool, reading the result, deciding what comes next — through four dedicated nodes with native approval support. The pipeline stays the default and costs 4 to 8× fewer tokens; you switch from the chat header. Each turn starts from a clean data registry, and the agent is told to fetch an exact value rather than recall an approximation. Two guardrails frame the loop: its deadline is measured on compute time, so waiting for your approval no longer eats into it, and a tool re-called identically is refused, then ends the turn.

proactiveInitiative.title: 🎯 Proactive Initiative
proactiveInitiative.description: Once the request is done, the assistant looks at whether the results reveal a connection worth mentioning: rain forecast on Saturday, so what outdoor plans are in the calendar? The evaluation receives candidate connections pre-computed from the semantic type registry, and prepares the final answer's context in parallel to keep latency down. It is strictly read-only — whether a tool may run here is decided by its declared category, never guessed from its name — so the initiative can look things up but can never change your data on its own.

telephony.title: 📞 Agentic Telephony
telephony.description: LIA can place outbound calls through a goal-directed voice agent, driven by your own credentials. Data protection is enforced by capability, not by prompt: the call agent gets a single read-only availability tool returning free/busy slots — never titles, attendees or locations. Nothing is recorded and no transcript is kept; a signed webhook posts a short summary back into the chat when the call ends. You confirm every call before it dials, and the agent works under a strict mandate: no expense or commitment beyond the objective, and anything offered outside it is surfaced in the recap.

todayBriefing.title: 🌅 Today Briefing
todayBriefing.description: The home page is a daily briefing: a personalised greeting and a short synthesis above nine cards — weather, agenda, unread mail, birthdays, reminders, health, “For you”, pending tasks, latest documents. No LangGraph chain here: independent fetchers run in parallel, each section cached with a TTL matched to how fast it really changes, and the fast cards are split from the LLM synthesis so the page renders progressively. Seven of the nine render nothing until their source is configured: instead of invisible holes, one line names them and links each to the setting that switches it on.

peers.title: 🤝 Peer Connections
peers.description: Two users of the same instance connect through a single canonical pair row with claim-once transitions, so duplicate requests and races cannot happen. Privacy holds by construction: a blocked, unknown or cooling-down target answers a byte-identical 404, so existence can never be probed. A relayed message is a draft you confirm, delivered by the recipient's own assistant with their personality and memory. Shares are field-level, read-only and re-validated at execution time — free/busy or details, task titles — and written to a pruned access log.

relations.title: ⭐ Personal CRM — Relations
relations.description: A lens, not a database: the Relations page gathers what LIA already knows about a person — open commitments, calls, memories, relayed messages — with an identity resolved by folding accents and case, and a confidence that is shown rather than assumed. Every section carries its exact total, computed over the whole set rather than read off the length of a page. Three sections come from the connected accounts — address book, mail, meetings — found by address and not by name, each with its own cache and a stated window. Launching a 360° from the card sends the invoked capability as data, so the tool lands on the right person.

provenance.title: 🔍 Provenance of conclusions
provenance.description: A memory claims you prefer morning meetings; a journal entry concludes on a mood. Each carries a bounded reference to the signals behind it: conversation, turn, date, and one of three roles — origin, evidence, contradiction. What is stored is a pointer and a timestamp, never the words: a copy would be a second permanent home for content you can delete elsewhere, and your deletion would stop being one. Deleting a conversation therefore empties the reference and leaves a dated row — a marker saying a signal existed, without bringing it back. The trail is capped at five references, and the cap is published in the response.

capabilityMap.title: 🌌 Capability map
capabilityMap.description: A star chart of what the assistant can actually do for this account. Each capability is a star — filled when genuinely usable, outlined when waiting to be set up — and its size comes from what it holds: four hundred memories shine brighter than three. A capability the instance disabled is absent, never greyed out. Nothing published is a level or a percentage: “three connectors linked” is a fact, “62 %” would be a competition. The drawing is decorative — every destination is a named link, reachable from the keyboard, and a narrow screen gets the same map as a list.

selfHosting.title: 🏠 LIA on your own machine
selfHosting.description: LIA is free software (AGPL-3.0) you can run on your own machine, depending on nobody. A guided installer asks a short questionnaire in your language — how you want to reach it, which provider keys you hold — builds the images from the source you cloned, applies the reference data in a single transaction, creates your administrator account, then checks the installation genuinely works: one migration head, reference data present, keys decryptable. A server that answers is not a successful installation. No secret travels through the command line, and a failed step resumes exactly where it stopped.

platformCapabilities.title: 🎛️ What this instance offers
platformCapabilities.description: Not every LIA instance offers the same features, and that is deliberate. Ten capabilities — dictation, speech, images, uploads, document spaces, web search, browsing, skills, MCP, telephony — are switched on or off by the administrator from the settings, with no redeploy and no configuration file. A capability that is off also disappears from the catalogue the planner sees: LIA never promises an action it cannot perform, so you never get a refusal after the fact — the answer says so plainly, in your language.

plugins.title: 🧩 Agent Plugins (open standard)
plugins.description: LIA is a conformant client of the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 open standard (steered by AWS, Microsoft, OpenAI, Cursor and Vercel, adopted by ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and VS Code): one portable package bundling skills and MCP servers. A plugin installs from a zip or a hardened https URL through the same pipeline as individual skills — staged extraction, zip-bomb and path-traversal guards, atomic install with rollback — and returns an exhaustive per-component report rather than a silent partial success. Components keep their plugin provenance, so an update preserves configured credentials and a plugin can never be silently amputated.

tabularAdmin.title: 📗 Administration by workbook
tabularAdmin.description: A screen holding a hundred entries is not edited one dialog at a time. A declarative description of the workbook — its sheets, its columns, their referentials — drives both directions: the export writes the file, the import reads it back. Columns are matched on hidden technical keys, so reordering them in Excel, hiding one, or exporting in one language and re-importing in another changes nothing. The import commits in two steps: the first writes nothing and returns the diff field by field, the second re-derives that plan and refuses if it moved. A row missing from the file never deletes anything — removal is an explicit column.

adaptiveThresholds.title: 🎚️ Per-user adaptive thresholds
adaptiveThresholds.description: A fixed similarity threshold is structurally unfair: the score distribution depends on each user's vocabulary and stock. A controller therefore learns a per-user threshold under four non-negotiable rails: hard bounds, hysteresis (one small step per day at most, whatever the error), observability (every adjustment counted, the effective value published in the debug panel), and a kill switch that freezes everything back to the static defaults. The state is advisory — a read failure falls back to the default, never to an error — and convergence was simulated on the real production distribution before activation.

expressiveEyes.title: Expressive eyes
expressiveEyes.description: A pair of cartoon eyes driven entirely by signals the app already emits — the chat state machine, execution steps, approvals, voice, the psyche engine. Twenty expressions, a reaction to each answer read from the model's own emotional self-report, an idle life of blinks and saccades, and six selectable looks. No extra LLM call and no new endpoint: the eyes are a free ride over existing telemetry.

nativeApps.title: 📱 Native Android & iOS apps
nativeApps.description: One published app per store, a client for any self-hosted LIA server: the app loads your server's own web interface, whose address you type at first launch — so web releases reach it instantly, with no store update. Sign-in leaves for the system browser (the only way Google permits) and returns through a deep link redeemed against a secret only the app holds. Notifications are native on both platforms and deliberately asymmetric: Android talks to your server's own Firebase project, while iPhone is woken through a stateless relay that says one fixed sentence and never learns who was woken or why.

selfDiagnostics.title: 🩺 Self-diagnostics & incident memory
selfDiagnostics.description: LIA reads its own telemetry through clients that never fail a request: every outage becomes a typed “unavailable” result. A periodic self-check evaluates the golden signals plus direct probes into health snapshots with exact values; alerts and critical verdicts converge into one incident per problem, diagnosed by a budget-capped model that is handed the threshold the value actually crossed, and writes in each administrator's own language. Administrators get a health panel, notifications and read-only chat tools — and a known outage shapes the answers: degraded capabilities are routed around at planning time, and a failed step is explained from typed error codes, never raw logs.

ephemeralScripts.title: 🧮 Computed answers, not guessed ones
ephemeralScripts.description: Ask how long your layovers add up to, which people appear in two lists, or what a set of figures comes to across timezones, and an AI answers plausibly — with nothing in the reply to tell you it is wrong. In its autonomous mode LIA now writes a few lines of Python and runs them in a locked-down sandbox instead: no network, no database, nothing beyond the data the turn already collected, a throwaway container each time. The answer was computed, not estimated. It stays a complement — most questions never need it — and administrators can read every script that ran, with its purpose and its output.

changelog.title: Version History
changelog.description: LIA functional updates version by version

v1_38_3.title: v1.38.3 — 🧠 The memory that was quietly going missing

items.i1: 🧠 LIA stops quietly losing what it just learned — in one hour of real use, nearly half of the operations that store a conversation in memory, index a message or fetch a document context were being refused by the provider, and nothing said so: the answers arrived normally, only slightly less well informed. The background tasks now start at staggered times instead of all at once, wait their turn when needed, and try again on a temporary failure.
items.i2: 📊 Platform Health now watches this — nothing measured whether these operations actually succeeded, only how many were attempted, which says nothing once failures are retried. A dedicated indicator and an alert have been added, with a procedure telling an administrator which of the two levers to pull.
items.i3: 🌍 Incident diagnoses in your own language — an incident's analysis and recommended actions were always written in English, on a page where every other word is translated. They are now written in the language of each administrator who reads them.
items.i4: 🔍 Diagnoses that finally say something — they used to answer "insufficient evidence to determine the exact cause" almost every time. That was accurate: the analysis was given a number without the threshold it had crossed, and a number alone cannot be judged. It now receives the unit, the verdict and both alert levels.

v1_38_2.title: v1.38.2 — 🙂 A face that answers the tone, not the habit

items.i1: 🙂 LIA's face answers the TONE of her reply — after every message the avatar wore roughly the same pleased expression, including after an error or a long technical explanation. LIA now states the register of what she has just written — warm, assured, factual, apologetic, curious, concerned… — and the face plays it. Twelve distinct expressions instead of one, and only two of them smile: a technical answer keeps a focused face.
items.i2: 👄 An expressive mouth — the avatar now has a mouth that carries the expression: it opens, deepens, leans to one side and follows the face. It arrives at the corners first, the way a real smile does, instead of appearing all at once.
items.i3: 🛠️ Deployment fix — on some installations a monitoring container refused to start after an update, with a permission error on its start-up script. Fixed, and an automatic check now stops the case from coming back.

v1_38_1.title: v1.38.1 — 🎨 Settings you can find at a glance

items.i1: 🎨 Every settings family has its own colour, every setting its own icon — the page listed fifty-three sections that all drew the same blue icon on the same blue chip, and sixteen of them borrowed another section's drawing on top of that (one plug shape served four different settings). Colour cannot separate a repeated shape, so both were fixed: a distinct icon per setting, and one colour per family — twelve colours you learn, not fifty-three you decipher. It works the same way in the sidebar, which is the settings list on a phone.
items.i2: ♿ The colour never carries meaning on its own — the section you have open still stands out by its background, its weight and the accent colour, not by being a thirteenth hue; and whether a capability is on is still shown by a filled or hollow dot. Anyone who does not perceive these colours loses nothing. Each of them was measured against every theme — light, dark and OLED, across the five accent colours — before shipping.

v1_38_0.title: v1.38.0 — 🎭 A full palette of moods, and a deployment that stops lying

items.i1: 🎭 LIA is no longer stuck in a single register — her mood mechanics rested every personality on the assertive side of the scale, so five calmer moods stayed out of reach at rest, and an internal pulse crowned joy the dominant emotion regardless of what she had actually appraised: measured over 90 days of production, 31% of turns, and up to every single turn for a light user. Both settings are now active: half the personalities rest in a calmer register, and the emotion shown is the one LIA really appraised. Assertive characters stay assertive.
items.i2: 📊 No measurement stays invisible to administrators — a metric no dashboard displays is a metric nobody acts on: a context source failing silently once dropped health signals for a week with nothing to flag it. An automatic check now verifies that every measurement LIA produces reaches a dashboard, a rule or an alert, and two new Grafana panels cover heartbeat source health and skipped cache writes.
items.i3: 🚀 The deployment says what it knows — and stops leaving your secrets behind — for self-hosters: going to production used to end on an error you had to learn to disregard, because a dropped connection was indistinguishable from a real failure. The deployment now runs on the server, independently of your terminal: closing the laptop or losing Wi-Fi no longer interrupts it, and the closing message finally tells a real failure apart from a lost contact. Along the way, the decrypted secrets file is wiped from your machine on every exit path, errors included.

v1_37_0.title: v1.37.0 — 🧮 Answers that were computed, and a sandbox that finally has its tools

items.i1: 🧮 LIA computes instead of guessing — when a question needs arithmetic over many rows, a comparison between two lists or durations across timezones, the assistant now writes a few lines of Python and runs them in a locked-down sandbox: no network, no database, nothing beyond the data already collected, and a throwaway container each time. The answer was computed, not estimated. It remains a complement: most questions never need it. Administrators can read every script that ran, with its purpose and output, in the debug panel.
items.i2: 🧩 The QR-code skill works again — and every other skill that needs a library. Scripts ran with the standard library only, because the sandbox account could not enter the directory holding the installed packages: the shipped QR-code skill could not load the library that draws the codes. Found by running a real script on the live server rather than by a test, and now guarded so it cannot come back.

v1_36_0.title: v1.36.0 — 🧮 LIA can now compute instead of guessing

items.i1: 🧮 A short script instead of mental arithmetic — an AI answers questions like "how long are my layovers in total", "which of these people appear in both lists" or "what does this add up to across timezones" plausibly, and nothing in the answer shows you it is wrong. When a step needs that kind of work, LIA now writes a few lines of Python and runs them in a locked-down sandbox — no network, no access to your data beyond what the turn already collected, a throwaway container each time — and answers with a result you could check. It stays a complement: most answers never need it, and it is deliberately told not to use it for anything it can answer directly. Administrators see every script that ran, in the debug panel.

v1_35_0.title: v1.35.0 — 🔎 A search that gets cut short now says so

items.i1: 🔎 No more “give me a minute, I'll get back to you” — when a long search hit its internal limit, the assistant sometimes ended the turn on the sentence it had written just before continuing, which read as a promise of work that never came: a turn ends when its answer is sent, so there was nothing to wait for. Now an interrupted investigation gives you what it DID find, says in one sentence that it was cut short and what is missing, and offers to continue — and it can no longer announce future work it will not do.
items.i2: 🧠 Your standing instructions now reach the autonomous mode too — in the step-by-step reasoning mode, long-term memory never reached the reasoning itself: the rules you had recorded about how the assistant should work could only influence the final wording, not the decisions. The same memory the other mode uses is now present where the decisions are actually made. Deep searches also get more room: the assistant keeps going as long as it keeps finding things, instead of stopping on a fixed count.

v1_34_1.title: v1.34.1 — 📌 Your standing instructions are remembered again

items.i1: 📌 “Rules & directives” memories can finally be created — long-term memory has a category for the standing instructions you give about how LIA should work (“answer me more briefly”, “always start with the conclusion”). The screen that shows them shipped, but nothing could ever fill it: the parser that turns an extraction into a memory rejected that exact category, and the rejection was logged at debug level — so the whole family was dropped in silence. The vocabulary now has a single source of truth, checked at startup against all three places that restate it, and a rejected memory is logged as a warning.
items.i2: 🩺 The platform can now say when it has lost the outside world — LIA watches its own health, and it met a real outage the day it shipped: the machine stopped routing traffic for its containers, so every call to an external service failed while the site itself stayed up and healthy. LIA reported the symptoms within six minutes, but nothing could name the cause. An administrator can now enable a small outbound-connectivity check that says it plainly, and each health figure is shown with the unit the server declares instead of one the screen guessed.

items.i1: 🩺 Platform health, inside the product — administrators get a new Settings panel showing what LIA continuously measures about itself: per-check verdicts with exact values, firing alerts, degraded capabilities with their suggested fallbacks, and an incident history. When something critical opens, the administrators are notified in-app and by push.
items.i2: 🔎 “LIA, diagnose yourself” — in chat, an administrator can ask LIA for its own health, a curated platform metric, bounded service logs or an incident's stored diagnosis. Each incident can carry an automatic diagnosis grounded on the operations runbook for that alert, with a probable cause and recommended actions — proposals for a human, never executed on their own, and capped by a daily budget.
items.i3: 🛟 Honest answers under failure, for everyone — when a step fails during a request, LIA now tells you precisely what succeeded, what failed and why, and applies a known workaround when one exists (for example switching web-search provider when one of them is down) instead of failing on a timeout.

v1_33_2.title: v1.33.2 — 📘 Self-hosting: the upgrade path, written down

items.i1: 📘 Moving your own installation to a new version — self-hosting the assistant, you had no written way to move an existing installation to a newer release. There is one now: seven steps, with the database backup first because migrations apply the moment the new container starts and there is no way back, and a rollback that restores the previous version in seconds. LIA can walk you through it if you ask her.
items.i2: ✅ The documentation now has to be true — every version number and threshold written in the docs is recomputed from the code that owns it, and a mismatch stops the build. Six documents were quoting six different wrong values for the same setting; that class of error can no longer reach you. The figures published on the public pages follow the same rule: recomputed, never carried over.

v1_33_1.title: v1.33.1 — 📍 Location settings in their own section

items.i1: 📍 A standalone "Location" section — your position sources (live geolocation, remembered last-known position, home address) leave the Google Places connector card for their own section under Preferences. This data always lived on your account, never on a connector — it now looks the way it works. Find it instantly by typing "address" or "GPS" in the settings search.
items.i2: 🧭 The FAQ points to the right place — several answers still directed you to "Settings > Connectors > Google Places" to configure your location; every language edition now points to the new section.

items.i1: 📱 LIA in your pocket — one official app per store, working with any self-hosted LIA server: you type your server's address at first launch, and that's it. The interface is the same as the web app, so every improvement reaches the app instantly, with no store update.
items.i2: 🔐 Google sign-in works in the app — and fixed a real flaw on the way: signing in with Google used to skip the two-factor code entirely. The code step is now enforced everywhere, app included.
items.i3: 🔔 Notifications on both platforms — Android talks directly to your server's own notification project: nothing passes through anyone else. iPhone requires going through the app publisher (an Apple rule, not ours), so a minimal relay wakes the phone with a fixed neutral sentence — your actual messages never leave your server, and the relay never learns who was notified or why.
items.i4: ↩️ Connecting services returns to the app — linking Gmail, a calendar or an MCP server from the app now brings you back into the app when done, instead of leaving you stranded in the browser.
items.i5: 📴 A real offline screen — if your server is unreachable, the app shows its own screen with a retry button and, crucially, a way to change servers: a mistyped address no longer means reinstalling the app.
items.i6: 🧪 Verified on real devices — an automated bench drives the actual app on an emulator through ten scenarios, from first setup to forgetting a server. It caught three real bugs before anyone else could.
items.i7: 📖 A complete publication guide — for anyone who wants to publish their own build: accounts, signing, both stores' forms, step by step with no prior knowledge assumed.

v1_32_0.title: v1.32.0 — 🧠 One way to ask a model to think

items.i1: 🧠 Reasoning depth becomes one clear setting — every model now offers the same ladder, from “no thinking” to “maximum”, with the levels that particular model actually accepts. Before, the same instruction was stored two different ways depending on the provider, and the admin screen could offer a depth the model's API refused — the save went through and the call failed later.
items.i2: 🎛️ The dropdown only offers what works — the list of depths, the option to switch reasoning off, the token budget: all of it now comes from the same source the server validates against. A model that cannot stop thinking no longer pretends it can, and a depth a model does not accept is no longer selectable.
items.i3: 🔍 The model catalogue says where its numbers come from — each row now shows whether its capabilities were corroborated by the public registries, verified by a human, or never curated at all. Announced retirement dates appear next to the models concerned, with the source of the information.
items.i4: 🧹 Two obsolete settings removed from the catalogue form — they described how the reasoning control used to be drawn, and nothing had read them since. A field you can edit that changes nothing is worse than no field.
items.i5: 🎚️ Accepted depths are ticked, not typed — the LLM Pricing screen shows the depths the model's family actually offers, and you untick the ones this particular model refuses. Everything ticked means "no restriction". A free-text field used to invite writing a level that does not exist, and it was dropped in silence.
items.i6: 📗 The Excel workbook writes reasoning directly — two columns replace the "copy the shape of another model" template, which could remove depths without saying so when it came from another family. On import, a depth outside the family is refused while naming the ones that would have been accepted. Creating a model that does not reason no longer requires picking a reasoning template.
items.i7: 🔧 Fixed: a depth restriction can be widened again — re-ticking every depth did not restore the full ladder: the previous restriction silently survived.

v1_31_3.title: v1.31.3 — 🌑 A truly black black, and landmarks recovered

items.i1: 🌑 OLED mode arrives — a perfectly black background, the one at which an OLED screen's pixels actually switch off: less battery drawn, and noticeably easier on the eyes at night. The header's theme button becomes circular: light, dark, absolute black, then light again. The switch is revealed by a circle opening from the button — skipped entirely if you have asked your system to reduce motion. Your five colour themes are untouched: only the neutral surfaces darken.
items.i2: 🎨 The display mode is now chosen in Settings — Appearance offers Light, Dark, System and an "Absolute black" switch. "System" follows your device and is reachable again: it is what every new account starts on, and the header button alone could never return to it. The OLED switch is only active in explicit dark mode, rather than changing your mode without telling you.
items.i3: ⌨️ Keyboard focus is visible again — three checkboxes (remember me, terms acceptance) showed no outline at all when reached with the keyboard, leaving no way to tell where you were in the form. They had no accent colour either. Fixed, and the outline now follows your theme.
items.i4: 👀 Two unreadable texts fixed — the badge marking that a skill answered was practically invisible in light mode, and its animated sheen stayed frozen over the word when animations are reduced. The quietest section headings — "try for example", the trace headers — were also too pale to read comfortably.
items.i5: ⚡ Lighter pages, and no more flicker — the nine selectable fonts were all downloaded on every visit, 618 KB for the single one displayed; only 162 KB remain, with identical rendering. And your colour theme is now applied before the first paint: the brief blue flash on load is gone. A missing page finally answers in your language.

v1_31_2.title: v1.31.2 — 🔎 Document search finds its answers again

items.i1: 📄 Your documents answer again — search across your knowledge spaces was discarding one correct answer in three: ranking mixed meaning-based understanding with keyword matching, and the second signal could eliminate a perfectly relevant excerpt purely because it shared no word with your question. Asking "is my data encrypted?" returned nothing, while five passages answered it. Fixed.
items.i2: 🌍 In all six languages, Chinese most of all — the defect hit harder the further your question's language sat from your documents'. On Chinese-language documents, search found the right answer only 7% of the time; it now succeeds nearly 9 times out of 10. French, German, Spanish and Italian all improve markedly.
items.i3: 🤫 Fewer off-topic excerpts — when your message has nothing to do with your documents, LIA now slips fewer of them into its reasoning than before. The fix improves relevance and reduces noise at the same time; it does not trade one for the other.
items.i4: 🛡️ A startup that refuses an inconsistent configuration — if the semantic-search model is misconfigured, the application says so at boot instead of letting every write fail silently in production. The debug panel also shows the relevance threshold in force, drawn directly on each score bar.

items.i1: 👥 Your contact groups are recognised — "email the family group" now works: LIA finds your Google Contacts labels, expands them into addresses and shows the exact member count. It can also find someone you have exchanged with but never saved.
items.i2: 📅 Free slots and video calls — "find me 30 minutes on Thursday" computes real availability from your calendar, reading only your busy ranges and never the content of your meetings. And a meeting created as a video call carries its Meet link (or Teams, depending on your provider) — announced only if it was actually created.
items.i3: ✉️ Your Gmail mailbox becomes steerable — "is my auto-reply on?", "turn on my out-of-office from the 24th to the 30th with this message", "archive and label everything from this sender". As with every send, the preview shows the exact wording before anything is written, and nothing happens without your approval. You will be asked to reconnect Gmail once.
items.i4: 📊 Your spreadsheets and documents become readable… and writable — "read my budget and answer", "summarise these minutes", then "add this expense" or "append this note". The preview shows exactly the rows or text to be written; no new permission is requested.
items.i5: 🌿 Weather answers the question you did not ask — with the Google Environment connector on, a plain weather question also brings air quality and in-season pollen, on the chat card and on your home page. The index shown is your country's when one exists, with the category the service itself publishes — never an in-house interpretation.
items.i6: 🛡️ Safety and freshness — every web address LIA is about to open is checked against Google's threat lists, and a flagged page is refused. On freshness, calendar, files and messages can now tell LIA when they change instead of being polled periodically (an administration option, off by default).

v1_31_0.title: v1.31.0 — ⚙️ The engine room moves to Python 3.14

items.i1: ⚙️ A modernized foundation — the whole assistant now runs on Python 3.14 and Debian 13, everywhere: your data is processed by a faster, current, long-supported runtime. Every one of the 229 underlying components was verified for the new platform before the switch — including on the little ARM server the public instance runs on.
items.i2: 🎙️ Telegram voice messages made future-proof — the audio layer that turns your voice notes into text relied on a piece Python removed in its newer versions; it was replaced before anything could break, and the exact audio conversion is now covered by automated tests so it can never regress silently.
items.i3: 🛡️ Guards that keep it that way — new permanent checks verify on every change that all parts of the system agree on the same Python version and that every native component loads correctly. A future upgrade that forgets a spot now fails loudly in development instead of quietly in production.
items.i4: ⚡ A fairness bug in the rate limiter is fixed — under simultaneous bursts, the shared request counter could let a few extra calls through its limit (two requests landing in the same microsecond collided). Reviving a long-dormant stress test surfaced it; the window now counts every request exactly, so quotas mean what they say.
items.i5: 🧭 The instance now reports its true version — the running server used to display a placeholder build identity in some deployments; the deployment script now reconciles it automatically, so what you see in diagnostics is exactly what was shipped.
items.i6: 🧹 Leaner and future-proof — five unused libraries were removed from the runtime (a smaller attack surface and faster installs), and every use of Python APIs scheduled for removal in future versions was modernized ahead of time. Test coverage grew again: the stress suite that found the limiter bug now actually runs.

v1_30_16.title: v1.30.16 — 👀 LIA looks back at you

items.i1: 👀 Expressive eyes in the chat — a small pair of cartoon eyes now lives on the chat page and reacts to everything: they watch your typing, squint while LIA thinks, scan while it searches, and react to each answer's emotional tone. Left alone they blink, look around, doze off progressively — and once in a while pull a genuine prank (they may even swap places).
items.i2: 🎨 Six looks to choose from — Cozmo glowing screens by default, plus Capsules, Marbles, Almond, Strokes and Rings with a moving pupil. Pick yours with live animated previews in Settings › Personalization › Eyes style.
items.i3: 🖐️ Fully yours — drag the eyes anywhere (arrow keys work too), resize them, or dismiss them to a tiny restore dot. By default they sit between the search field and the knowledge badge, and they always return exactly where they belong.
items.i4: 🧹 A lighter chat header — the amber “Processing…” pill and the little wait phrase are gone: the eyes now carry that state, and they say more (thinking, searching and answering are three different looks). The offline pill stays — that one tells you something the eyes cannot.

v1_30_15.title: v1.30.15 — 🛡️ Sturdier in the real world

items.i1: 🔔 Smarter notifications across tabs — the tab you are actually using always keeps its live connection; a long-forgotten tab can no longer pile up dead connections behind the scenes. Come back to a tab and it reconnects on its own.
items.i2: 🌍 Weather for any place name — an unknown or misspelled location now gets a clear "location not found" answer (with a second geocoder trying first), instead of a technical error.
items.i3: 🔎 Deep web research gets the time it needs — long syntheses are no longer cut off at 30 seconds, and an over-long search query is automatically shortened instead of failing.
items.i4: 🔒 Cleaner, more private technical logs — asking for your confirmation is no longer counted as an error, and draft content or recipient names never end up in the technical logs.
items.i5: 📊 For admins: honest showroom metrics — the demo funnel counts every mission again, clicks toward the free live instance are now measured, and a new alert watches for Redis connection-pool saturation.

v1_30_14.title: v1.30.14 — 👁️ The invisible work becomes visible

items.i1: 🕐 New Activity page — everything LIA did for you, as one chronological feed: notifications sent, interest discoveries, journal notes, detected habits, tracked and closed commitments, executed routines. With exact totals, never approximations.
items.i2: 💡 Proposals awaiting your go — the Alerts hub gains a “Proposals” section: routines LIA offered to handle that you haven't decided on yet. “I'm on it” opens the chat prefilled — nothing is sent without you. “Not now” teaches it to insist less.
items.i3: 📌 Say it once, it sticks — “answer shorter”, “stop suggesting that in the evening”: your instructions become durable rules, visible and editable in your memories (“Rules & directives” category). And when you correct LIA, it acknowledges once, without triple apologies — it simply changes.
items.i4: 🧠 A memory that dates its recollections — LIA can naturally say “last week you told me…”. And when a fact changes (you move, you switch jobs), the old one is no longer overwritten: it archives cleanly behind the new one and never resurfaces in searches.
items.i5: 🔊 Your briefing reads itself aloud — a Listen button on the morning synthesis, and a voice whose expressiveness follows the assistant's mood. If synthesis fails, you get a clear message — no more silent failures.
items.i6: 📈 Your habit streaks count — “9 days in a row, 7-day milestone reached, next: 30” in the Habits panel. And under chat suggestions, LIA now says why it proposes (“because you follow…”).

items.i1: 🔕 Notifications finally respect your ongoing conversations — the "don't interrupt an active user" rule existed in the configuration but never actually applied: it now genuinely checks your latest message before any proactive send. Mid-discussion, LIA waits its turn.
items.i2: 🎚️ The assistant tunes its own working memory, for you — the threshold deciding when a journal note deserves to enter a reply now adjusts per user, inside strict bounds, at most one small step per day, with a kill switch. Your vocabulary isn't someone else's: neither is the setting.
items.i3: 📓 The journal truly learns from your reactions — the "note → apply → observe your reaction → confirm or correct" loop is unblocked end to end: consolidation no longer stalls on small journals (the portrait stays fresh), and a note can no longer declare itself "validated" without real evidence.
items.i4: 🧭 Habits: the detection bar is shown in plain sight — when no activity window is detected, Settings now display the bar actually applied (it is stricter on weekends, where observed days are fewer). No more unexplained "no habit detected".
items.i5: ⚖️ Fair proactive distribution — account selection on each notification cycle is now randomized and filtered in the database: no account can be silently left behind the others anymore, and accounts that disabled the feature no longer consume a slot.

v1_30_12.title: v1.30.12 — 🧱 A typed foundation under every conversation

items.i1: 🧱 The run context is now typed and verified — the "who, where, with which preferences" of every conversation used to travel in a 17-key bag with no contract; it now rides in a typed block validated at the graph's entrance: if it is missing, the application refuses instead of carrying on silently — including when resuming a pending confirmation.
items.i2: 🌍 A sub-assistant inherits the whole context — language, timezone, consented location: the hand-made copy that kept only 6 values out of 17 is replaced by full inheritance. A German-speaking profile can no longer get a sub-assistant answering in French by default.
items.i3: 🛡️ The tool contract facing the model is continuously guarded — every tool must prove it presents itself correctly to the model, with no internal parameter leaking; two new automatic guards lock that contract, and the orchestration libraries are up to date.

v1_30_11.title: v1.30.11 — 📊 Model pricing is administered in Excel

items.i1: 📊 The whole pricing grid exports, edits and re-imports in one go — the 124 models and their tariffs download as a structured Excel workbook: a translated usage notice, dropdown lists, cell validations and a referentials sheet.
