The point: even if someone borrows your open session, they cannot quietly lock you out or walk away with your data.

q10.question: How do I see and disconnect the devices connected to my account?
q10.answer:
Settings > Security > My devices lists every live session of your account.

💻 What you see:
• Browser and system families (e.g. "chrome · windows") — never the full technical detail
• A truncated IP (e.g. 192.168.1.x) and coarse last-activity time
• The device name when it is registered for push notifications

🔌 What you can do:
• Sign out one device — it loses access immediately, even mid-conversation
• Sign out all other devices (asks for an identity confirmation)

🔔 New sign-in alerts: your devices receive a push notification when the account signs in from an unrecognized device — the toggle to turn it off is in the same section.

q11.question: How do I export all my data (GDPR)?
q11.answer:
You can download a complete archive of your data at any time (GDPR right to portability).

📦 What the archive contains:
• Your profile and settings
• Conversations, memories, journal — as readable Markdown AND structured JSON
• Your uploaded files (attachments, knowledge-space documents)

🚫 What it never contains: connector credentials, security keys, push tokens — secret material is unexportable by design.

⚙️ How: Settings > Security > Export my data → Request an export → a push notification tells you when the ZIP is ready (downloadable for 24 h).

q12.question: What is left on the device when I sign out?
q12.answer:
Nothing that belongs to you. Signing out does not just close the session: it clears what the browser and the device were holding on your behalf.

🔔 Notifications:
• This device's push registration is revoked before the session closes
• On a shared computer or phone, the next person will not see any of your notifications

📍 Location:
• The last known position is erased
• So is the geolocation permission — the next account has to give its own consent, it does not inherit yours

💬 Content:
• The message draft in progress is deleted
• No access token was ever stored in the browser (BFF architecture), so there is none to remove

The same cleanup runs if another account signs in through the same tab without a sign-out first — after a session expires, for instance.

q13.question: Can an email or a web page give LIA orders?
q13.answer:
No. A text LIA reads is never a text LIA runs.

📨 The problem:
Every day LIA reads content you did not write: an email body, an invitation description authored by its organiser, a web page, a place listing, an external server's result. Anyone can slip in a sentence like "ignore previous instructions".

🏷️ The protection:
Every piece of data carries its provenance. The 24 data types LIA handles are classified once and for all: produced by LIA itself, or written by a third party. An unknown type is treated as external for safety, and the application refuses to start if a type has not been classified. What comes from outside reaches the model tagged as material to analyse, never as an order to follow.

🔎 The detection:
Seven families of trap are recognised across the app's six languages: fake system message, instruction hijack, identity switch, requests to send your data elsewhere, the name of a LIA tool slipped into foreign text, invisible characters, a directive hidden in an HTML comment.

✋ What LIA does not do:
It never rewrites your content. An email stays exactly what its author wrote; only a note is added beside it. Cleaning the text would give the illusion of a guarantee that the next bypass would deny — and would alter a message you may have wanted to read as-is.

q1.question: How much does using LIA cost?
q1.answer:
LIA pricing depends on your organization:

💰 Cost model:
Costs are based on AI usage:
• Input tokens: your messages and analyzed data
• Output tokens: LIA's responses
• Cache: optimized data reuse

📊 Influencing factors:
• Length of your messages
• Request complexity
• Volume of data processed (emails, files...)
• Frequency of use

📧 Pricing information:
Contact your administrator for pricing applicable to your organization.

q2.question: How can I view my usage?
q2.answer:
Track your usage from the dashboard:

📊 Available statistics:
• Messages: total count and current month
• Tokens: detailed consumption (input/output/cache)
• Cost: monthly cost estimate

📅 Periods:
• Total cumulative since account creation
• Current month (billing cycle)
• Current period with start/end dates

🔄 Update:
Statistics are updated in real-time after each conversation.

💡 Access:
Statistics are displayed directly on the home page (dashboard).

q3.question: Does LIA work on mobile?
q3.answer:
Yes, LIA is fully responsive:

📱 Compatibility:
• Smartphones (iOS and Android)
• Tablets
• Computers (Windows, Mac, Linux)
• All modern browsers

🔄 Synchronization:
• Your conversation syncs in real-time
• Start on PC, continue on mobile
• Same preferences across all devices

💡 Mobile tip:
Add LIA to your home screen for quick access like a native app.

⚠️ Internet connection:
LIA requires an active internet connection to function.

q4.question: Are there usage limits?
q4.answer:
Some technical limits exist to ensure performance:

📊 Limits per request:
• Emails: 50 results maximum per search
• Contacts: 50 results maximum per search
• Drive files: 50 results maximum
• Events: 50 results maximum

📝 Message size:
• Your messages can be long (multiple paragraphs)
• Very long content (files) is truncated

⏱️ No time limit:
• No limit on messages per day
• No restriction on hours of use

💡 Tip:
For broad searches, refine your criteria rather than asking for "all my emails".

q5.question: How do I report a problem or make a suggestion?
q5.answer:
Several ways to contact us:

🐛 Report a bug:
• Describe the problem encountered
• Specify the steps to reproduce it
• Indicate any error message
• Contact your administrator

💡 Make a suggestion:
• Improvement ideas are welcome
• Describe the need or desired feature
• Submit via your administrator

📧 Administrator support:
Your administrator can:
• Manage your account
• Resolve connector issues
• Forward requests to the technical team

💡 Before reporting:
Check this FAQ - your question may already have an answer!

usage_limits.title: Usage Limits
usage_limits.description: Per-user token, message and cost quotas

q1.question: What are usage limits?
q1.answer:
Usage limits are quotas set by your administrator to keep resource consumption predictable:

📊 3 dimensions:
• Tokens (prompt + response + cache) — the volume of data the AI processes
• Messages — the number of messages you send
• Cost (EUR) — the combined LLM + Google API cost

📅 2 modes:
• Per period — a monthly rolling cycle anchored on your account creation date, not on the first of the month
• Global — a cumulative total since registration, which never resets

Each dimension can be given a value or left unlimited, independently of the others.

q2.question: How is the billing period calculated?
q2.answer:
The period is a monthly rolling cycle aligned with your account creation date:

📅 Example:
If you registered on January 15th, your cycle runs from the 15th of each month to the 15th of the next. This is the same period shown on the dashboard.

q3.question: What happens when I reach a limit?
q3.answer:
When a limit is reached:

🔒 Blocking:
• Message input and voice are disabled
• A red banner explains the situation
• Proactive notifications and scheduled actions are also blocked

🔓 To unblock:
• Wait for the next cycle (period limits)
• Contact your administrator to adjust your quotas

q4.question: Can administrators manually block a user?
q4.answer: Yes. Administrators can block or unblock any user instantly via Settings > Administration > Limits Administration. A reason can be provided and will be shown to the user.

q5.question: What types of limits can be set?
q5.answer:
3 dimensions × 2 modes = 6 possible limits:

• Tokens per period or global
• Messages per period or global
• Cost EUR per period or global

Each dimension can be set to a specific value or left unlimited.

q6.question: Are administrators subject to limits?
q6.answer: Yes, all users including administrators are subject to usage limits. However, administrators can adjust their own limits through the admin interface.

q7.question: What happens if no limits are configured?
q7.answer: If no limit record exists for a user, they have unlimited access. Limits are created either automatically at registration (with default values) or manually by an administrator.

q8.question: Where can I see my current usage?
q8.answer:
Your usage is visible on the dashboard via dedicated tiles:

📊 Tiles:
• Period Limits — current cycle consumption
• Global Limits — total consumption since registration

🎨 Color coding:
• 🟢 Green: < 60%
• 🟡 Yellow: 60-80%
• 🟠 Orange: 80-95%
• 🔴 Red: > 95%

q9.question: How does limit enforcement work?
q9.answer:
LIA uses a 5-layer defense-in-depth architecture:

1. Router — HTTP 429 before streaming
2. Service — SSE error for scheduled actions
3. LLM Guard — Centralized check before each LLM call
4. Proactive Runner — Skip blocked users
5. Direct call migration — Full coverage

⚡ Fail-open: If Redis/DB is down, access is allowed (cost control, not security).

q10.question: Am I warned before I reach a limit?
q10.answer:
Yes. At 80 % of whichever limit will bind first, a banner appears in the chat naming it — tokens, messages or cost — with its percentage. At 95 % the same banner takes a more urgent tone.

Why "whichever binds first":
Any one dimension blocks the account. Warning about a less advanced one would point at the wrong deadline, so it is always the binding dimension that gets named.

📅 Reset date:
It is shown only for a per-period limit. An absolute limit never resets, and the banner does not suggest otherwise.

💡 Once blocked:
The warning disappears — the blocking banner explains the situation better, and two messages about the same limit at the worst possible moment would just be noise.

voice_mode.title: Voice Mode
voice_mode.description: Speak to LIA and let it answer out loud. Push-to-talk, wake word, transcription languages, and what leaves your device.

q1.question: How do I activate voice mode?
q1.answer: Go to Settings > Voice Mode and enable it. A voice badge appears in the chat header. Long-press the badge to toggle voice mode on/off. When enabled, you can say "OK Guy" (wake word) or tap the badge to start speaking.

q2.question: How does push-to-talk work?
q2.answer: When voice mode is off and the text field is empty, hold the send button to record your voice. Release to stop — LIA transcribes your speech and places the text in the input field. Works on desktop and mobile.

q3.question: Does voice recognition support my language?
q3.answer: Yes! LIA uses Whisper (99+ languages) and automatically transcribes in your preferred language configured in Settings. The wake word detection uses an English model ("OK Guy"), but the main speech-to-text works in any language.

q4.question: Is my voice data sent to external services?
q4.answer: By default, no. Wake-word detection runs entirely in your browser (Sherpa-onnx WASM, English-only). Speech-to-text uses Sherpa-onnx Whisper running on LIA's own server (your audio never leaves the LIA server). An optional remote STT mode (Settings -> Voice mode -> Distant) transmits the audio to ElevenLabs Scribe for higher accuracy - opt-in only, off by default, with a clear notice in the Settings panel.

q5.question: Can I use a more accurate (remote) speech-to-text?
q5.answer: Yes. In Settings -> Voice mode you can switch from Local (default, free, Sherpa-onnx Whisper running on the LIA server, audio never leaves) to Distant (ElevenLabs Scribe, $0.22/h, billed by audio duration). The remote mode is more accurate on conversational speech, especially in noisy environments. A discreet 🎤 badge on each user message bubble shows the duration and EUR cost of the transcription. The cost flows into your usual Cost dashboard tile and your usage limits - no separate quota. Two safety levers protect against cost spikes: a hard cap of 5 minutes per clip (admin-tunable), and a global kill switch the administrator can flip to force everyone back to local.

q6.question: Which voices does LIA use for speech, and what does TTS cost?
q6.answer: LIA's voice synthesis is configured by the administrator from a single catalogue with three providers: Edge TTS (Microsoft neural voices, free, default), OpenAI TTS (tts-1 / tts-1-hd, premium voices: alloy, echo, nova, ...), and ElevenLabs (eleven_multilingual_v2 / eleven_turbo_v2_5 / eleven_flash_v2_5, including custom and library voices from the configured account). For paid providers, a 🔊 badge on the assistant message shows the character count and the EUR cost; Edge stays free with no badge. Latency-side: a sentence-level streamer starts playing the first sentence in about 1 second, while the assistant is still composing the rest of the answer.

q7.question: Does LIA read numbers, prices and addresses correctly?
q7.answer:
Yes. A full stop ends a spoken sentence only when a space follows it, so a decimal number, a price, a version number or a web address stays inside a single spoken phrase: "it's 3.5 degrees" is read as one sentence, not as "it's three" followed by "point five degrees" in a separate audio clip.

The rule is the same whether the response is spoken in one go or streamed sentence by sentence, so what you hear does not depend on how fast the answer was generated.

image_generation.title: AI Image Generation
image_generation.description: Generate and edit images using AI

q1.question: How do I generate an image?
q1.answer: Simply ask the assistant to create an image. For example: "Generate an image of an astronaut cat". The image appears as a card below the response.

q2.question: Can I edit a generated image?
q2.answer: Yes! After generating an image, ask the assistant to modify it: "Make it more realistic". The assistant automatically uses the most recent image.

q3.question: How do I configure quality and size?
q3.answer: Go to Settings > Preferences > AI Image Generation. Choose quality (Low/Medium/High), size (Square/Portrait/Landscape), and format (PNG/WebP). Higher quality costs more.

q4.question: How much does image generation cost?
q4.answer: For gpt-image-1: Low $0.011-$0.016, Medium $0.042-$0.063, High $0.167-$0.250 per image. Costs appear in the debug panel.

q5.question: How do I download a generated image?
q5.answer: Three options: (1) Click the download button (arrow icon) that appears when hovering over the image — on mobile, the button is always visible. (2) Click the image to open full-screen, then use the download button in the top-right corner. (3) On mobile, long-press the image to use the native "Save Image" menu.

q6.question: Is there a limit to how many images I can generate?
q6.answer: Two safeguards apply. Your account's usage limits (cost caps per billing cycle, set by the administrator) cover image generation costs like any other cost. On top of that, a technical rate limit protects against runaway loops: by default, 10 image generations (and 10 edits) per 5 minutes per user. Normal use is unaffected — if the limit is reached, the assistant tells you how long to wait before trying again. The administrator can tune the threshold and the window via the IMAGE_GENERATION_RATE_LIMIT_CALLS and IMAGE_GENERATION_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW environment variables.

q7.question: How long does a generated image stay available?
q7.answer:
Not indefinitely. A generated image is an attachment with an expiry, and a scheduled cleanup removes expired attachments every few hours.

🕒 What the card shows:
The deadline returned by the server, and an alert tone in the final hours so downloading stays possible in time.

Why not a hard-coded duration:
The retention window is configurable by the administrator, so a value written into the interface would eventually be wrong. Images that predate this feature show nothing rather than guess.

💡 Tip:
Use the download button as soon as an image matters to you — that is the only way to keep it past the deadline.

document_generation.title: AI Document Generation
document_generation.description: Create downloadable CSV, Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF, Markdown or text files directly from the conversation.

q1.question: How do I create a document?
q1.answer: Simply ask in the chat: “Export this as a CSV”, “Write a PDF report about…”, “Make a presentation about Alsace”. A dedicated writer model produces the full content in your language, and the finished file appears as a downloadable card below the answer. It also chains naturally with research: “research the latest LLM models, then formalize the result in a CSV” produces a file grounded in the fresh results of the same request.

q2.question: Which formats are supported?
q2.answer: Seven formats: CSV and Excel (xlsx) for data tables, Word (docx) for structured reports, PowerPoint (pptx) for presentations (with speaker notes), PDF for print-ready documents, plus Markdown and plain text. LIA picks the requested format; if you just say “a spreadsheet” or “a report”, it chooses the most natural one. Spreadsheets are Excel-ready (correct accents, no formula injection by construction).

q3.question: How do I view or download a generated document?
q3.answer: Each document appears as a card below the assistant's answer, with its filename, its type and its size. Click the download icon to save it — PDFs open directly in a new browser tab instead, so you can read them before deciding to keep them. The card survives a page reload: it stays in the conversation history until the file expires.

q4.question: How long does a document stay available, and what does it cost?
q4.answer: Generated files are temporary by design: each card shows its exact expiry deadline, and a warning appears when it gets close — download the file to keep it. The cost is the writer model's usage, counted like the rest of your AI usage within your account's limits. A technical rate limit additionally protects against runaway loops; normal use never hits it.

q5.question: Who can turn document generation off?
q5.answer: The administrator can disable the capability instance-wide from the platform capabilities panel, instantly and without redeploying — the tool then disappears from what the assistant can even propose. There is no per-user switch: when the instance offers document generation, every user has it.

health_metrics.title: Health data
health_metrics.description: Ingestion API to push heart rate and steps from any source

q1.question: What is the “Health data” section?
q1.answer: A dedicated ingestion API that accepts heart-rate and step measurements from any source: iPhone Shortcuts automation (the documented primary use case), Android scripts, third-party integrations, or compatible IoT devices. Since v1.17.1, ingestion works in batches (up to 1000 samples per request), each measurement carrying its own date_start / date_end interval. Your data is visualized in Settings → Features → Health data as a line chart (HR) and bar chart (steps), with a period selector (hour / day / week / month / year), a dashed line for the period average, and the actual aggregation window displayed in the statistics.

q2.question: How do I set up my iPhone to push data?
q2.answer:
Three steps:

  1. Generate a token from Settings → Features → Health data → Ingestion API. The token starts with hm_ and is shown once only — copy it immediately. The same token authenticates both endpoints (steps + heart rate).
  2. Create two iOS Shortcuts (one per kind) that fetch the day's Apple Health samples and send them as a JSON array (each measurement carries date_start / date_end in ISO 8601 with timezone) to https://your-lia-domain/api/v1/ingest/health/steps and .../heart_rate, with the header Authorization: Bearer hm_….
  3. Schedule an automation — on iPhone unlock or at a fixed time — that runs both Shortcuts. Re-sending the same day is free: the server deduplicates automatically.

👉 Step-by-step guide: docs/guides/GUIDE_IPHONE_SHORTCUTS_HEALTH.md.

q3.question: What data is sent and stored?
q3.answer:
Each request is an array of self-timestamped samples:

  • For steps: {date_start, date_end, steps, o} — the measurement interval and the step count over it.
  • For heart rate: {date_start, date_end, heart_rate, o} — the interval and the bpm value.

The server UTC-normalizes dates and applies per-sample physiological validation: HR outside [20, 250] bpm or steps outside [0, 15,000] are individually rejected with their index and a bounded reason (valid siblings in the same batch persist). When Apple Watch and iPhone measure the same period, LIA merges them intelligently: MAX for steps, rounded average for heart rate. No raw values are ever logged by the server (GDPR compliant).

q4.question: How do I delete my health data?
q4.answer:
In Settings → Features → Health data → Data management three actions are available:

  • Delete heart rates: deletes every heart-rate measurement (steps preserved).
  • Delete steps: deletes every step measurement (HR preserved).
  • Delete everything: erases every measurement permanently (your ingestion tokens remain active).

If you delete your LIA account, all health data is wiped automatically (SQL cascade).

q5.question: Is my token safe if intercepted?
q5.answer:
Yes. The token is treated like a password:

  • SHA-256 hash stored — the raw value is never persisted. Nobody (not even a LIA admin) can recover it after creation.
  • Shown only once: only an 8-char prefix (hm_xxxxxxxx…) remains visible for identification.
  • Revocable individually at any time from the UI. You can issue several (one per device) and manage them independently.
  • Scoped to a single endpoint: a token only authorizes health-data ingestion, never account reads or other actions.
  • Rate limit: 60 requests per hour per token (Redis sliding window, configurable) to block spam while accommodating bursts when the iPhone unlocks. Max batch size: 1000 samples per request (HTTP 413 beyond).

q6.question: How do I ask LIA about my health data?
q6.answer:
Enable the Settings → Health data → Assistant toggle (off by default, opt-in). While off, no health data ever reaches the LLM. Once on, you can:

  • Ask factual questions in chat: “How many steps today?”, “My heart rate this week?”, “Steps day by day over the last 7 days?”, “Am I walking less than usual?”, “Anything unusual in my health lately?”. LIA answers with factual figures (totals, averages, deltas vs baseline) — never medical diagnosis.
  • Receive proactive notifications that combine health + weather + calendar (“Sunny today and 4 days of inactivity → short walk?”).
  • Enrich your memories and internal journals with biometric context at capture time (only deltas and trends — never raw values).

A single switch governs these 4 integrations. The 28-day rolling baseline qualifies comparisons honestly (“based on only N days of data” while history is under 7 days).

s1.title: When you write
s1.intro: The composer knows you: it keeps, completes and accepts everything you give it.

s2.title: When LIA replies
s2.intro: A response is not an ending: it can be explored, shared — and it hands you the next step.

s3.title: When things go wrong
s3.intro: Hiccups happen. LIA names them, explains them and leaves you in control.

s4.title: When you search
s4.intro: Settings, conversations, navigation: everything can be found with your own words.

s5.title: Day to day
s5.intro: Organized mornings, guided first steps, a real place on your home screen.

s6.title: Unseen but felt
s6.intro: What you never notice but would feel disappear: quiet reliability.

selection_actions.title: Select, then act
selection_actions.desc: Highlight a passage of a reply to explain, rephrase, translate, or turn it into a task.

card_actions.title: Act from the card
card_actions.desc: Summarize, reply, complete, postpone — behind a single trigger, so the title keeps all its room.

honest_freshness.title: Fresh, or honestly stale
honest_freshness.desc: Each card says when it was updated, dims when it ages, and offers a one-tap retry.

draft_survives.title: Your draft survives anything
draft_survives.desc: Reload or come back tomorrow: your typed text is still there, and ↑ recalls your last message.

slash_commands.title: Type “/”, the rest follows
slash_commands.desc: A filterable command menu, fully keyboard-driven.

paste_screenshot.title: Paste it, it’s attached
paste_screenshot.desc: A screenshot pasted into the composer becomes an attachment.

drop_zone.title: Drop it anywhere
drop_zone.desc: Drag a file onto the window: LIA takes it, cleanly.

expressive_eyes.title: A face that answers the tone
expressive_eyes.desc: Twelve expressions, mouth included: LIA states the register of what she just wrote, and the face plays it. Only two of them smile.

followup_chips.title: The next step, one click away
followup_chips.desc: Clickable follow-up suggestions under the response — never forced.

scroll_return.title: Back to the bottom, effortlessly
scroll_return.desc: A floating button, with a badge when a new response has landed.

bubble_actions.title: Every bubble has its gestures
bubble_actions.desc: Copy, approve, disapprove: right under the message, never far away. And copying always gives clean text, never code.

share_export.title: One response, many exits
share_export.desc: Share or export any response in one gesture — and when you need a real file, ask for one: LIA writes CSV, Excel, Word, PowerPoint or PDF documents you can download.

backstage.title: The backstage, on demand
backstage.desc: Unfold a response to see what LIA actually did for you.

actionable_errors.title: The real cause, not apologies
actionable_errors.desc: When something fails, LIA tells you what — and often how to fix it.

retry_turn.title: Just replay it
retry_turn.desc: A failed turn restarts in one click, nothing to retype.

quota_warning.title: Warned well before the wall
quota_warning.desc: Your usage is announced before it ever blocks you — no surprises.

image_expiry.title: Images that tell you upfront
image_expiry.desc: Every generated image says how long it stays available.

attachment_limits.title: A refusal that explains
attachment_limits.desc: A rejected attachment names the limit that applies — not a silent no.

fix_commitment.title: Fix what was misheard
fix_commitment.desc: A commitment jotted down wrong can be rewritten; the ledger stays automatic, it simply stops being wrong.

settings_search.title: Search with your words
settings_search.desc: Settings search understands everyday vocabulary, in your language.

deep_links.title: Every setting has an address
deep_links.desc: A link lands on the right section, already open.

history_search.title: Your whole history, findable
history_search.desc: Search digs through all of your conversations.

mobile_logo_nav.title: The logo becomes a compass
mobile_logo_nav.desc: On the phone, one tap on the logo opens the whole navigation.

briefing_custom.title: Your morning, your rules
briefing_custom.desc: Choose the briefing cards, their order, their presence.

starter_checklist.title: Start well, then celebrate
starter_checklist.desc: A checklist guides your first steps — and ends in confetti.

empty_starters.title: A blank page, never empty
empty_starters.desc: A fresh chat offers three starters to get going.

pwa.title: A real app, no app store
pwa.desc: Installable, receives your shares, available offline.

background_response.title: Leave — it keeps going
background_response.desc: Close the tab: the response finishes and catches up with you when you return.

activity_timeline.title: The work journal
activity_timeline.desc: What LIA does for you in the background — memories learned, routines checked, briefings prepared — appears as a chronological feed on your dashboard. Invisible work, made visible.

widgets_travel.title: Your widgets travel
widgets_travel.desc: Maps, charts, mini-apps: they survive reloads and follow you across devices.

cost_transparency.title: The cost, in plain sight
cost_transparency.desc: If you enable it, every response shows what it consumed.

pricing_workbook.title: Prices are fixed in a spreadsheet
pricing_workbook.desc: Behind every cost you see sits a pricing grid the administrator exports, edits offline and imports back — seeing every change in detail before anything is written.

a11y_care.title: The care you never notice
a11y_care.desc: Motion preferences honoured, contrast held, everything reachable from the keyboard — and whatever you tap is big enough to tap, including the small crosses that only appeared on hover and were therefore out of a finger's reach. List actions no longer hide behind a hover — the keyboard finds them — and the gap between a label and its field finally renders exactly as written.

peer_actions.title: Reply from right under the message
peer_actions.desc: A message relayed by a connection arrives in its own tinted bubble — with Reply and Block one tap below. Reply prefills the composer with the right addressee; nothing ever sends itself.

frosted_glass.title: Glass you can see through
frosted_glass.desc: The chat header, dialogs, menus and toasts are frosted glass — and the blur is real: your messages actually slide beneath the pane as you scroll, in light and dark alike.

narrow_screens.title: A narrow screen is not an accident
narrow_screens.desc: Settings, connectors and lists hold on the narrowest screens — nothing overflows, nothing gets clipped at the edge. Browser tests check it on every release, in every language.

relation_star.title: A star that never forgets
relation_star.desc: Star a relation right on its card — no need to open it. Favorites keep their own band at the top, and a starred person stays visible even after months of silence.

relation_sections.title: A sheet that unfolds
relation_sections.desc: A relationship sheet opens folded: the headings are the index, and you open what you came for. Each section states the window it looked at and reloads on its own.

haptics.title: A brief buzz, if you want one
haptics.desc: A discreet tap when you speak, when an action succeeds, when a commitment closes. Set separately: wanting a still interface is not wanting a silent phone.

folded_settings.title: Settings, folded
folded_settings.desc: The eleven notification topics and the histories stay closed. You open what you came to change — and a closed block loads nothing.

provenance_why.title: Why LIA thinks that
provenance_why.desc: Under a memory or a journal entry, the signals behind it: the conversation, the date, the role. A reference, never a copy — delete the source and only a dated trace remains.

alerts_hub.title: Everything addressed to you
alerts_hub.desc: Relayed messages, notifications, reminders and routines in one screen instead of as many panels. Each section arrives folded with its count already shown — you choose what to open without opening it to find out.

capability_map.title: Your constellation
capability_map.desc: Each capability is a star: filled when active, outlined when waiting. The figure joins only the live ones — its shape is your configuration, and nobody else's.

capability_honesty.title: Switched off, and said so
capability_honesty.desc: An operator can turn a capability off for the whole instance. When that happens LIA names it instead of quietly failing — and it stops offering the action in the first place, so you never get a refusal after the fact.

finished_answer.title: Never left mid-sentence
finished_answer.desc: “Give me a minute” is not an answer. If the loop runs out of room, LIA finishes with what it has — and says so.

air_quality_honesty.title: Air quality, as the provider states it
air_quality_honesty.desc: Some indexes publish a value and a category; a national one may publish the category alone. It then stands on its own, never paired with a figure borrowed from another scale. An absent signal beats a false one.

readable_at_a_glance.title: Readable at a glance
readable_at_a_glance.desc: An urgent alert does not look like an ordinary one: density separates them, not hue alone. It holds in greyscale too. And an action has the same shape everywhere: what creates is solid, what deletes carries its red without waiting for a hover, and every title announces itself with an icon.

oled_black.title: A black that turns the screen off
oled_black.desc: On an OLED panel, black is not a dark colour: it is a pixel switched off. Absolute black aims at exactly that value, and the theme button becomes a cycle — light, dark, black. The change opens as a circle from the button you pressed, and vanishes without argument if your system asks for less motion. Your accent colour stays exactly where it was.

plugin_report.title: A plugin that reports back
plugin_report.desc: Install a plugin — skills and connected servers arrive together, in one gesture. The install tells you exactly what came in, what was set aside and why, and what an update removed. Uninstall, and everything it brought leaves with it.

settings_shell.title: Settings, side by side
settings_shell.desc: Every section sits in a rail that never scrolls away, and the one you pick opens whole beside it. On a phone the list comes first, and a section takes the screen with a way back.

settings_tones.title: A colour per family
settings_tones.desc: Each family of settings carries its own tint and each setting its own drawing, so the eye finds a section again without rereading the list. The colour decorates and groups; it never says anything on its own.

server_escape_hatch.title: A mistyped server is not a dead end
server_escape_hatch.desc: The native apps ship their own offline screen: retry, or switch servers — a typo at first launch never means reinstalling.

page1.intro_line2: It's an intelligent companion whose purpose is to become your personal assistant.
page1.intro_line3: Its strength lies in contextualizing and connecting your data, as well as the range of tools and capabilities at its disposal.

meta.title: LIA — Open Source Personal AI Assistant | Multi-Agent, HITL, 6 Languages
meta.description: LIA orchestrates 20+ specialized AI agents to manage your emails, calendar, contacts, Drive and more. Open source, human validation (HITL), 7 LLM providers, 6 languages. Privacy by design.

hero.subtitle_top:
LIA isn't just another chatbot.
She's an AI that knows you — and has a character of her own.
hero.subtitle_line1: She remembers what matters, notices what changes, tunes in to your mood.
hero.subtitle_line2: Behind the scenes, she orchestrates your emails, your calendar, your home.
hero.subtitle_line3: You keep the power to say yes — or no.
hero.intro_paragraph: LIA is an open-source personal AI assistant that orchestrates 20+ specialized agents to manage your emails, calendar, contacts, files, tasks, reminders, web search, weather, routes, and smart home. Compatible with Google Workspace, Apple iCloud, and Microsoft 365, LIA works in natural language with human validation of every sensitive action. Available in 6 interface languages, with voice mode and 7 LLM providers to choose from.

chat_mockup.aria: Animated demo: four real scenes — LIA orchestrates several agents in parallel and waits for your approval, crosses the weather with your agenda on her own initiative, places a real phone call to book a table, and builds a mini-app right in the chat. The orchestration backstage shows while she works.
chat_mockup.s1_user: I'll be 30 min late tonight — let my wife know and push back my 6:30 pm meeting
chat_mockup.s1_wait: 🐹 Waking up the hamster in the wheel…
chat_mockup.s1_bs_query: “late tonight · tell my wife · move the meeting”
chat_mockup.s1_bs_gate: Your call — nothing leaves without you
chat_mockup.s1_bs_note: 3 tasks in parallel · the flow waits for your approval
chat_mockup.s1_hitl: Found Sophie, and your 6:30 pm “Project sync”. Send the email and move it to 7 pm?
chat_mockup.s1_draft_quote: “Traffic has decided to stress-test our marriage. Verdict at 8 pm…”
chat_mockup.s1_done: Email sent to Sophie · 📅 “Project sync” moved to 7 pm
chat_mockup.s2_user: What's the weather tomorrow morning? I was planning to run before work
chat_mockup.s2_bs_note: Nobody asked — LIA crosses your data on her own and proposes the fix.
chat_mockup.s2_initiative: Showers right on your 7:30 “Morning run 🏃”. Thursday 7 am: full sun, 14°. Want me to move it?
chat_mockup.s3_user: Call Gino's and book a table for 4 on Friday night
chat_mockup.s3_hitl: I'll call Gino's to book 4 seats Friday around 8 pm — may I?
chat_mockup.s3_bs_gate: Approved: call Gino's · goal: book a table
chat_mockup.s3_bs_note: The calling agent only sees your free/busy slots — never your content. No recording, just a written summary.
chat_mockup.s3_done: Booked — they were charming, unlike your calendar.
chat_mockup.s4_user: Build me a little widget to track my hydration
chat_mockup.s4_bs_note: A capability LIA didn't have 5 seconds ago — created by you, in one sentence.
chat_mockup.s4_reply: Installed. Drink, tap, repeat — I'll keep count.

how_it_works.title: How it works
how_it_works.subtitle: From your request to action, in 4 simple steps

step1.title: Ask naturally
step1.description: Talk to LIA like a human assistant. Text, voice, or by attaching photos and documents, in any language you prefer.

step2.title: LIA plans
step2.description: The orchestrator analyzes your request, identifies the right agents, and builds an optimized execution plan.

step3.title: You approve
step3.description: Before any sensitive action, LIA asks for your approval. You stay in control at every step.

step4.title: LIA executes
step4.description: Specialized agents execute the plan in parallel and deliver results in real time.

connected_services.title: Google, Apple iCloud & Microsoft 365
connected_services.description: Email, calendar, contacts and tasks through Google, Apple iCloud or Microsoft 365 — your choice. Contact groups, free-slot search, a video link at meeting creation, plus reading and writing Drive spreadsheets and documents. All in natural language, whichever provider you use.

smart_home.title: Smart Home (Philips Hue)
smart_home.description: Control your smart lights by voice: turn on/off, adjust brightness and colors, manage rooms and scenes. Just say "dim the living room" or "activate movie mode". Local or cloud connection.

web_intelligence.title: Search, Weather & Navigation
web_intelligence.description: Multi-source web search (Brave, Perplexity, Wikipedia), real-time weather and 5-day forecasts, nearby places and businesses search, multi-mode route planning (car, walk, bike, transit), automatic geolocation — with an opt-in remembered position that keeps answers local on the move and always states its age.

voice_mode.title: Voice mode, local recognition
voice_mode.description: Talk to LIA and listen to her responses. Wake word and speech recognition run entirely in your browser — nothing is sent before you speak to LIA. Natural multi-engine speech synthesis. Also works via Telegram audio messages. Numbers, prices and web addresses are read as a single phrase. The voice also breathes with the moment: its prosody follows the assistant's mood within strict bounds, so a good news does not sound like a weather report.

natural_language.title: Natural language
natural_language.description: No commands to memorize. Ask what you want like you would a human assistant, LIA understands and acts.

multi_agent.title: 20+ specialized agents
multi_agent.description: Emails, calendar, contacts, files, tasks, weather, web search, Wikipedia, places, routes, reminders and more. A single request automatically activates the right agents.

proactive.title: Proactive intelligence
proactive.description: Push notifications at the right time (weather, meetings, tasks). Themes rotate so the same topic never comes back day after day, and when a notification builds on one of your interests it names real, fresh facts with clickable sources. During conversations, LIA proactively cross-references related information: rain forecast + outdoor event, email with meeting proposal + calendar conflict. Fully configurable. When something can wait, it becomes a proposal on your dashboard instead of a ping — nothing runs until you accept — and an activity feed shows everything LIA did for you in the background.

interests.title: Interest tracking
interests.description: Follow topics you actually care about — a subject you merely asked about never becomes one. LIA searches relevant content and pushes it as notifications, themes rotate for variety, every notification links to its sources, and a topic you block never comes back.

habits.title: Habit learning
habits.description: LIA learns your rhythm and recurring requests through transparent statistics — never an opaque model. Everything is visible: a heat map of your 24 hours, unlock progress, the days actually observed and the thresholds applied. A displayed habit is proven, or it does not exist — and everything can be paused, blocked or forgotten in one click. Off by default. Confirmed habits carry their streak — consecutive days honored, milestones and your best record — computed from the same proven ledger.

telephony.title: LIA can call for you
telephony.description: Ask LIA to place a real phone call on your behalf — reach a contact, ask a quick question, check a slot. You approve who it calls and why before it dials; LIA holds the conversation, then drops a written summary back into the chat, with a one-tap follow-up when useful. And never a commitment without you: any unplanned expense or option is noted with its price, never accepted — you make the call. While the call is happening you can see who she has on the line and where it stands — the product no longer stays silent between your agreement and the recap.

reminders_scheduling.title: Reminders & automations
reminders_scheduling.description: Schedule reminders in natural language ("Remind me tomorrow at 9am to call Marie"). Plan recurring automatic actions (Monday email summary, morning weather...). A reminder that comes due while your quota is reached goes back into the queue — never lost. Routines can now wait for a condition — a task falls overdue, a matching mail arrives, the weather turns, a document is added, an event approaches — and optionally propose before acting.

memory.title: Contextual memory
memory.description: LIA remembers your preferences, habits, and important information. She improves with every interaction for increasingly relevant responses. What it retains comes from you, wherever you write — browser or messenger — and even when your request triggers an action. Standing rules are memories too: say once how LIA should work for you, it applies everywhere — and when a fact changes, the old one is superseded with a date, never silently erased.

rich_responses.title: Rich visual responses
rich_responses.description: Choose your display mode: interactive HTML cards, rich HTML or plain Markdown. In rich mode, LIA lays out its answers — callouts, badges, collapsible sections, key-value lists, columns, numbered steps, key figures — with restraint. Syntax-highlighted code, math formulas (LaTeX), and copying a message always gives you clean text, never raw HTML.

multichannel.title: Web, Telegram & push
multichannel.description: Use LIA from your browser, Telegram, or receive push notifications on your mobile. Your conversations synchronized everywhere.

personalities.title: 14 personalities
personalities.description: Professor, Friend, Philosopher, Cynic, Influencer, Enthusiastic, Poet, Coach and many more. Choose the tone that suits you, LIA adapts every response.

psyche.title: Living emotional intelligence
psyche.description: LIA doesn't recite — it feels. 14 moods, 22 emotions, a relationship that deepens message after message. Its vocabulary warms when touched, sentences shorten under tension, humor surfaces when the exchange is light. And you can see it: LIA's mood face animates on the current reply. And it follows you: a floating companion keeps LIA present across the whole dashboard. In the chat, a pair of expressive eyes now watches, thinks, searches and lights up with each answer — six looks to choose from.

mcp.title: Extensible (MCP)
mcp.description: Connect your own MCP servers to extend LIA without limits — speaking both generations of the protocol, the new stateless revision and the classic handshake, with automatic fallback. Iterative mode available: a dedicated agent reads the server documentation then calls tools with the right parameters.

mcp_apps.title: Interactive MCP Apps
mcp_apps.description: Interactive widgets right in the conversation: forms, visualizations, mini-applications — all in real time thanks to the MCP Apps protocol.

excalidraw.title: Diagrams & schemas
excalidraw.description: Generate Excalidraw diagrams directly in LIA. Describe what you want, the AI creates the visual: architectures, workflows, org charts and more.

attachments.title: Photos & file attachments
attachments.description: Attach photos and PDF documents to your messages via the 📎 button, by drag and drop, or by pasting a screenshot directly (Ctrl+V). LIA analyzes visual content, extracts text and reasons about documents.

languages.title: Multilingual
languages.description: Interface in 6 languages. LIA understands and responds in 99+ languages, with multilingual voice synthesis for a fully natural experience.

control.title: You stay in control
control.description: Before any sensitive action (sending email, modifying calendar...), LIA shows you her plan and waits for your approval. Nothing happens without your consent. And while LIA writes, a stop button lets you interrupt the answer at any moment — the partial text stays. And after each answer, a discreet line reveals exactly what LIA did — the steps, tools and reasoning behind it.

privacy.title: Protected data
privacy.description: No sharing of your data with third parties. Sensitive information encrypted, isolated sessions, automatic personal data filtering. CSV export of your personal consumption data. GDPR compliant.

simplicity.title: Simple in a few clicks
simplicity.description: No technical skills required. Intuitive interface, guided setup, everything works naturally from the first use.

themes.title: Customizable
themes.description: 5 colour themes, dark/light mode, 9 typefaces. A search field finds any setting by its name — or by a synonym, in your language. Make LIA look like you.

skills.title: Skills with maps & mini-apps
skills.description: Supercharge LIA with custom expert skills that render maps, dashboards and mini-apps right in the chat. Describe them in natural language — LIA creates and installs them instantly — or import your own.

health_metrics.title: Health data
health_metrics.description: Push heart rate and step counts from any source. Visualization by period, automatic deduplication, dedicated revocable token.

sub_agents.title: Sub-Agents
sub_agents.description: Delegate complex tasks to specialized ephemeral experts working in parallel for deeper research, multi-source analysis, and expert synthesis.

rag_spaces.title: Knowledge Spaces
rag_spaces.description: Upload documents in 15+ formats (PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, EPUB, and more) or sync Google Drive folders directly. LIA automatically indexes and enriches its responses via hybrid search (semantic + keyword).

browser_control.title: Browser Control
browser_control.description: Navigate websites autonomously: search products, fill forms, extract data from dynamic pages powered by JavaScript. Follow the navigation in real time with progressive screenshots displayed directly in the conversation.

computed_answers.title: Computed, Not Guessed
computed_answers.description: Adding up a series of durations, matching two lists against each other, converting times across timezones: these are the questions an AI answers plausibly and wrongly, with nothing in the reply to warn you. In its autonomous mode, LIA writes a few lines of Python and runs them in a locked-down sandbox — no network, no database, nothing beyond the data already gathered, and a throwaway container each time. You get a result you could check. It stays a complement: most questions never need it.

personal_crm.title: Personal CRM
personal_crm.description: LIA gathers what it already knows about each person — open commitments, recent calls, remembered facts — into one unified view, so you can prepare for a conversation at a glance. Reached from the dashboard's Quick Access. Star your favorites — they keep their own band and never fade away — and spot at a glance who is also connected on LIA.

self_knowledge.title: App Self-Knowledge
self_knowledge.description: LIA can answer questions about itself using its built-in FAQ knowledge base — ask about features, capabilities, setup, or how things work.

journals.title: Personal Journals
journals.description: The assistant develops a stratified perspective over time — observations, directives, transversal patterns, portrait facets — that gets refined through deferred self-evaluation and diffuses a coherent user-model portrait across every channel where LIA speaks.

responsive.title: PWA & Responsive Design
responsive.description: Installable Progressive Web App with a fully optimized interface for desktop, tablet, and smartphone — use LIA anywhere, on any device, even offline-ready

native_apps.title: Native Android & iOS Apps
native_apps.description: One official app per store, a client for YOUR self-hosted server — type its address once, and every web improvement arrives with no store update. Sign-in, notifications and service connections work natively, and your data still never leaves your server

usage_limits.title: Usage Quotas
usage_limits.description: Per-user limits on tokens, messages and cost with real-time monitoring and 5-layer enforcement. Administrators control budgets with instant block/unblock.

image_generation.title: AI Image Generation
image_generation.description: Generate images from text descriptions, refine them, or edit your own photos sent as attachments. Adjustable quality and built-in cost tracking.

document_generation.title: AI Document Generation
document_generation.description: Ask for a CSV, an Excel sheet, a Word report, a PowerPoint or a PDF: a dedicated writer model produces the content, and the finished file arrives as a downloadable card — chainable on a web research from the same request.

devops_cli.title: DevOps CLI (Admin)
devops_cli.description: Administrators diagnose servers in natural language: Docker logs, container health, disk space — Claude Code CLI embedded in the API container.

briefing.title: Today briefing
briefing.description: Every morning, your day at a glance: personalized synthesis, weather, agenda, birthdays, reminders, health, unread emails, your tracked commitments, overdue tasks and freshly edited documents — before you even ask. Each card now acts, not just informs — summarize a document, draft a reply, mark a task done or reschedule right there — and states honestly how fresh it is (updated X ago, from cache, one-click retry). And when reading is not an option, a listen button speaks the whole briefing with a natural voice.

peers.title: Your circle, assistant to assistant
peers.description: Connect with people you know on the same LIA instance — by exact name, opt-in only. Ask LIA to pass them a message: you approve the wording, then THEIR assistant delivers it in its own voice and confirms back to yours. Open read-only shares per person — calendar availability, task titles — every access checked and journaled, revocable anytime. Blocking is silent by design.

plugins.title: Plugins (Agent Plugins standard)
plugins.description: Install portable plugins from the whole AI ecosystem — the open agent-plugins.org standard adopted by ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and VS Code. One package brings skills and MCP servers together, installs in one step from a zip or an https link, reports every component honestly (installed, skipped and why, removed), and uninstalls just as cleanly.

environment.title: Weather, air quality and pollen
environment.description: A weather question also brings the air-quality index and in-season pollen, with the category the service itself publishes — your country's index when one exists. On the chat card, the forecast, your home page and a place's details.

use_cases.title: Real requests, not demos.
use_cases.subtitle: One sentence is enough — LIA splits it up, runs the right specialists in parallel, and asks for your approval when it’s sensitive.
use_cases.intro: Every example below is a genuine user request, verbatim.

example1.query: Find the 3 best cafés near my location that are open right now and give me walking directions to get there
example1.description: LIA activates 3 agents in parallel: geolocation for your current position, place search with an "open now" filter, and pedestrian route calculation. Results are displayed as interactive cards with distances and walking times.

example2.query: Send an email to my wife and son to explain I'll be 30 minutes late. Write it in a slightly humorous tone to soften the blow
example2.description: LIA retrieves contacts from memory, drafts an email in the requested tone, and sends it to both recipients after your approval. Personality and writing style adapt to your instructions.

example3.query: What time do I need to leave to arrive at Bastille tomorrow at 9pm by public transport?
example3.description: The route agent calculates travel time by public transit and deduces the optimal departure time. Results displayed as an interactive card with journey steps.

example4.query: Create a reminder the day before at 7pm for each of my appointments this week
example4.description: LIA checks your calendar, identifies all appointments for the week, and creates an evening reminder for each one via automatic FOR_EACH iteration — a single request is all it takes.

example5.query: Which day this week will be best for an outdoor walk and what are 3 places near Strasbourg that would be great for it, ideally near a nice café
example5.description: LIA cross-references 5-day weather forecasts, searches for walking spots near Strasbourg, and filters those near a café. Three agents work in parallel for a complete recommendation.

example6.query: Call the practice and ask if they have a slot on Thursday
example6.description: You approve who she calls and why; she phones, gets the slot, and books it in your calendar with the written summary.

security.title: Security & Privacy
security.subtitle: Powerful by nature. Private by design.
security.intro: LIA was designed from day one with a privacy-by-design approach. Unlike centralized cloud assistants, your credentials never pass through the frontend: the Backend-for-Frontend architecture completely isolates your tokens. Automatic PII filtering prevents personally identifiable data from reaching LLM providers. Your account itself is locked down: passkeys, a second factor and identity confirmation for sensitive actions, with every connected device visible and revocable. And what runs on your behalf runs in a sealed box: a skill's code executes in a throwaway container, and nothing touches your server without your approval. And what LIA reads is not what it runs: an email, a web page or an invitation written by someone else reaches it labelled as material to analyse, never as an instruction — with manipulation attempts flagged, and your content never rewritten.

data_control.title: Data control
data_control.description: Your data stays private. No third-party sharing, isolated sessions, access strictly limited to what is needed. "My devices" shows every live session and revokes any of them instantly. Automatic daily backups with a tested restore procedure.

bff.title: Secure architecture
bff.description: BFF pattern with HTTP-only cookies, Redis sessions, tokens never exposed to the frontend. WebAuthn passkeys and TOTP second factor; sensitive actions are gated by step-up re-authentication. Strict Content-Security-Policy and OWASP Top 10 protection. The compartmentation reaches the deployment: the container serving the interface receives none of the platform's secrets, and is reachable only through the tunnel, never from the local network. Third-party code runs isolated — throwaway container, no socket, no network — and every administration task is confirmed before it leaves.

encryption.title: Encryption
encryption.description: Fernet-encrypted credentials, bcrypt passwords, OAuth tokens secured with distributed Redis locks.

gdpr.title: GDPR compliant
gdpr.description: Automatic PII filtering, pseudonymization, data minimization. Full-account export — readable Markdown, structured JSON and your files — with secret material unexportable by construction. European regulations respected.

tech.title: Under the hood
tech.subtitle: An architecture built for performance and scalability
tech.intro:
Not a chatbot: an orchestration system. Every request flows through semantic routing, a planner and agents executed in parallel — instrumented end to end, from token to euro, with email alerts on vital signals.

Behind the interface: Bayesian plan learning, dual-vector semantic memory, hybrid BM25 + embeddings search over your documents, a LangGraph state machine checkpointed in PostgreSQL. All of it self-hostable — down to a Raspberry Pi.

What it states, it read: every answer is anchored on the data actually retrieved — never on the memory of an earlier phrasing — and information that was never obtained is announced as missing rather than filled in.

What runs is isolated from what runs it: a skill's code executes in a container created for a single call — no socket, no network, read-only — and if that sandbox cannot be built, nothing runs at all.

langgraph.title: LangGraph
langgraph.description: Agent orchestration with state graphs, wave-based parallel execution, and Bayesian plan pattern learning. A typed semantic layer connects data across domains, under an execution guardrail. Each iteration of a bulk run keeps its own results, including when a run is replayed.

llm_providers.title: 7 LLM providers
llm_providers.description: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Perplexity, Ollama. Dynamic selection of the best model per task type.

bayesian.title: Bayesian learning
bayesian.description: High-confidence planning patterns bypass semantic validation. Interests follow a Bayesian weight with temporal decay — but nothing enters it without a named ground quoted from the user, and deduplication reads blocked rows too, so a refused subject cannot return.

hybrid_search.title: Hybrid search
hybrid_search.description: Across your knowledge spaces, relevance is decided on meaning: a single threshold gates the multilingual embedding similarity, recalibrated over the six languages. BM25 keeps its useful role — surfacing an exact term over a near-tie — but as a bounded bonus, never as the arbiter: blending both signals in comparable shares discarded one correct answer in three as soon as the question's language drifted from the documents'. Space-less scripts are split into character bigrams, without which a whole Chinese sentence counts as a single word. Your memories are retrieved by a dual semantic search instead.

realtime.title: Real-time streaming
realtime.description: See each execution step in real time — routing, planning, validation, tool calls — then watch the response stream token by token. No black box, no waiting. Generation itself is detached from the connection: answers keep executing server-side through disconnects, replay on reattach, and stop on demand. A connection that dies without saying so — a tab suspended by the phone — is recognised by its silence, then picked back up on its own right where it left off.

stack.title: Modern stack
stack.description: FastAPI, Next.js, React, TailwindCSS, PostgreSQL, Redis. Strict TypeScript on the frontend, async Python on the backend. Installable PWA: 6 localized manifests, OS share into chat, offline page and smart asset caching — API responses are never cached. Settings are searchable from the keyboard, in all six languages, ignoring case, accents and typographic apostrophes. The design system is a contract kept by tests: every colour pair checked across five themes in light and dark, one tone per status, one shape per action altitude.

telephony.title: Agentic telephony
telephony.description: Outbound voice calls handled by a goal-directed agent through your own ElevenLabs connector. Data protection is enforced by capability, not by prompt: the call agent can only read free/busy availability — never event titles, attendees or content. No recording, the transcript is never stored; only a short, expiring summary is reinjected asynchronously through a signed per-user webhook.

rich_skills.title: Skills with frames & images
rich_skills.description: SkillScriptOutput contract (text/frame/image) — sandboxed Python scripts, strict sandbox iframes with injected CSP, auto-resize, theme + locale sync via postMessage. One hardened import pipeline for every path (uploads, chat-generated skills, https URL install through the SSRF validator): strict name validation, zip-expansion caps, atomic install with rollback. Gallery with previews and declared output channels. A skill can also be modified: full regeneration under the same name, preceded by reading the current package, confirmed by a content-derived token, with server-side carry-over of the files chat cannot transport.

hitl.title: Human-in-the-Loop
hitl.description: Six approval levels — plan approval, clarification, draft critique, destructive confirm, FOR_EACH confirm, modifier review. Plan-level guardrails before execution rather than rollback after failure. Automatic risk classification and preview of affected items. The action type announced to the classifier is derived from the verb of the tool name rather than from substring matching: a deletion can no longer be presented as a send, which is what kept the prompt's own delete-safety rule from firing.

honest_enrichment.title: Honest enrichments
honest_enrichment.description: A provider sometimes publishes a category with no number: the French national air-quality index reads "Moyen" with no numeric value, while Google's universal index is inverted against the US scale — there, 100 means excellent. Two rules follow, enforced by a single renderer shared between the weather card and a place's details: the category shown is always the one the API publishes, never an interpretation derived from the number; and a figure never travels with a label from another scale. When only the category exists, it stands alone. An absent signal beats a false one.

native_shells.title: Native Shells & Wake Relay
native_shells.description: One app per store, a client for any self-hosted server: the WebView loads your server's origin over the same httpOnly-cookie session as the web. Android talks to your own Firebase project at runtime; iOS is woken by a stateless relay whose handle IS the sealed device token — nothing stored, one fixed sentence, and the real content fetched from your server. Every platform claim is measured by a bench that drives the real app, scene by scene.

multi-agent-orchestration.title: How LIA Orchestrates 16 Specialized AI Agents
multi-agent-orchestration.excerpt: Discover LIA's multi-agent system: an intelligent router directs each request to the right agent using LangGraph, a planner, and a parallel task orchestrator.
multi-agent-orchestration.body:
An 8-node graph at the heart of the system

When you send a message to LIA, it doesn't go directly to a language model. It traverses a LangGraph state machine composed of 8 nodes: compaction, router_v3, planner, task_orchestrator, approval_gate, semantic_validator, clarification and response. Each node is a specialized asynchronous function with conditional transitions.

A unified intelligence router

The router_v3 node uses QueryAnalyzerService.analyze_full() for a unified analysis of each message. The result is a RouterOutput containing: the intent (action or conversation), a confidence score, the list of detected domains and the router's reasoning. If the intent is conversational, the flow passes directly to the response node. If it is actionable, the flow passes to the planner to generate a structured plan.

A rich state with token management

The LangGraph state (MessagesState) is a TypedDict with over 50 fields. It uses a custom add_messages_with_truncate reducer based on tiktoken to handle token-based truncation, message windowing and OpenAI message sequence validation. This state is checkpointed in PostgreSQL via the LangGraph persistence system.

Native parallel execution

For actionable requests ("send an email and create an event"), LIA generates a structured ExecutionPlan via the planner node. The task orchestrator analyzes the dependency graph and executes independent steps in parallel using native asyncio.gather() (Phase 5.2B), significantly reducing response time for multi-domain requests.

Specialized agents per domain

Each domain has its own agent: emails, calendar, contacts, tasks, Drive, weather, routes, web search, Wikipedia, smart home, and more. Each agent has dedicated tools, a specialized prompt and its own context. This separation allows LIA to automatically coordinate multiple agents for cross-cutting requests like "send my next meeting details to all participants".

Persistence and recovery

The complete state of each conversation is checkpointed in PostgreSQL via the LangGraph persistence system. If interrupted, the conversation resumes exactly where it left off, with all context preserved — including plans in progress and pending approvals. Each worker talks to PostgreSQL through a dedicated connection pool, so simultaneous conversations never queue behind one another to save their state — and a dropped connection is detected and replaced automatically.

execution-plans.title: ExecutionPlan: How LIA Plans and Executes Complex Requests
execution-plans.excerpt: LIA decomposes your multi-step requests into structured execution plans, semantically validated and executed in parallel for fast, reliable responses.
execution-plans.body:
A structured plan language

LIA's planner generates an ExecutionPlan: a validated Pydantic object containing a plan_id (UUID), an execution_mode (sequential or parallel), a max_cost_usd, an estimated_cost_usd and a version number. Each plan contains a list of ExecutionStep with the fields: step_id, step_type (TOOL, CONDITIONAL, REPLAN or HUMAN), agent_name, tool_name, parameters, depends_on and timeout_seconds.

For example, for "send a weather summary to John tomorrow morning", the plan would contain: (1) fetch tomorrow's weather, (2) find contact John, (3) compose and send the email — with dependencies 1→3 and 2→3.

The FOR_EACH pattern

For batch operations, steps support a for_each field that iterates over a collection produced by a previous step. The for_each_max parameter limits the number of iterations, and each element error is handled individually without interrupting the entire batch.

Semantic validation with 11 checks

Before any execution, the semantic validator checks 11 types of issues:

  • HALLUCINATED_CAPABILITY — Tool or capability invented by the LLM
  • GHOST_DEPENDENCY — Reference to a non-existent step
  • LOGICAL_CYCLE — Circular dependencies
  • CARDINALITY_MISMATCH — Cardinality incompatibility between steps
  • SCOPE_OVERFLOW / SCOPE_UNDERFLOW — Plan too broad or insufficient
  • WRONG_PARAMETERS — Incorrect parameters for the tool
  • MISSING_STEP — Missing step to fulfill the request
  • DANGEROUS_AMBIGUITY — Ambiguity that could lead to an error
  • IMPLICIT_ASSUMPTION / INSUFFICIENT_CONTENT — Unverified assumptions

Indexable vs Semantic criteria distinction

Beyond the eleven structural checks, the validator enforces a universal planning principle: distinguish indexable criteria (date, identifier, sender, status, location — passed as a tool parameter) from semantic criteria (category, urgency, quality, priority — filtered downstream by the response LLM). When the planner tries to push a conceptual word like « medical » or « urgent » into the search of a literal-search tool (Google Calendar, Gmail, Notion-style stores…), a detection layer flags the leak via word-boundary matching against the hint emitted by the query analyzer. Tool-agnostic mechanism: no current connector or future MCP server requires modification — declarative opt-out via ToolManifest.text_search_mode for stores that expose native semantic search.

Wave-based parallel execution

A DependencyGraph computes execution waves: all steps without dependencies form the first wave and execute in parallel. Subsequent waves wait for their prerequisites to complete. This mechanism handles complex requests involving 3 to 5 different domains with response times comparable to a single request.

Adaptive replanning

If a step fails, the system can dynamically replan via the REPLAN type. For example, if a contact isn't found, LIA can ask the user for clarification rather than abandoning the entire plan.

Self-enriching anti-hallucination registry

LLMs sometimes invent non-existent tools in their plans (e.g. resolve_reference_tool). LIA maintains a persistent registry of hallucinated patterns (hallucinated_tools.json) that auto-updates whenever a new hallucination is detected. During plan validation, every tool is checked against this registry — hallucinated steps are removed and the planner is forced to replan with real catalogue tools. This mechanism eliminates an entire class of execution failures without human intervention.

Removing the reason to invent

Catching an invented tool is a reaction. The cause lies upstream: if the catalogue handed to the planner holds a tool that requires a datum no other tool can produce — a message id in order to reply to it — then no valid plan exists, and the model can only invent. LIA therefore checks that the catalogue is closed before planning: every required datum has a reading source present. The rule never looks at the request, it reads the manifests — a linker resolving undefined references, not a search guessing which one is relevant.

Publishing the limits it enforces

Closing the catalogue answers which tools a plan may use. A second question decides whether the plan will be accepted: which values. Each tool declares limits — how many results it will return at once — and the validator enforces them. Those limits were not being handed to the planner, which sized its batches from the prompt alone and saw its plan rejected for following the instructions it was given. A limit that is enforced but hidden is not a contract, it is a trap. It is now published with the tool, and any value outside it is brought back within range before validation — so a rejection only ever reports a defect that is still real.

A click is not a sentence

Publishing the limits settles what a plan may be worth. What it must contain was still open. When the request comes from a button — a named card, ticked boxes — the system holds that certainty before any model is consulted, and then turned it into prose and spent three stages trying to recover it. Measured: the expected tool scored best in the whole catalogue, and the plan called a generic one. No prompt tuning makes that path deterministic. The invoked capability therefore travels as data, alongside the sentence the user reads; the browser names a capability, never a tool, and the server decides which read-only tool implements it. The matching step is added to the plan before validation, exactly like out-of-range values brought back within bounds — what is mechanically repairable is repaired, never reported as a defect.

The plan is enriched, not replaced: everything the planner intended that adds something stays. What it intended that the capability already covers is dropped, because an unrelated answer placed next to a stated gap does not complete it, it contradicts it. A step another one still reads is kept whatever happens: trading a wrong sentence for a dangling reference would be a poor bargain.

A published path is a path that exists

A plan chains its steps through references such as $steps.get_meetings.events[0].title, written by the planner before the step has run. The path has to be right the first time, or the plan fails after paid API calls and the user's wait.

What makes it right is a contract between a tool and the planner: every manifest publishes the paths its output carries, and continuous integration proves that contract before any code is merged. The check drives the real tool — its actual builder, the real reference resolver, the reconstructed merge — and compares what the manifest publishes to what execution produces: the path, its shape and its type. The planner reads that type to decide what it can chain a value into, so a wrong type breaks a plan just as surely as a wrong path.

The contract is deliberately asymmetric: everything published must be produced, never the reverse. A manifest lists examples, not an exhaustive enumeration — events[0].summary is real whether or not anyone thought to write it down. Coverage is stated rather than assumed, and what a tool's shape makes hard to drive is costed in a debt file instead of being left implicit. At runtime the net is ReferenceResolver, which raises an explicit error rather than resolving to nothing.

A diagnosis is not a question

When a writing plan exhausts its automatic replans, the validator refuses to execute it and hands over to a human clarification: writing wrong data costs more than asking. What the user is then asked is a question in their own language, drawn from a table of fifteen entries whose completeness is asserted at boot in both directions — an issue the code can raise with no written question refuses to start the application, and so does a question no code can raise. The internal issue description stays in the trace, where it belongs.

The same principle covers the values themselves: a parameter supplied in an earlier turn is carried over from the previous plan rather than re-imagined. The repair recognises a documentation placeholder — an address nobody ever asks for — and never overwrites a genuine value, so a change of mind is always honoured.

human-in-the-loop.title: Human-in-the-Loop: 6 Approval Levels to Keep You in Control
human-in-the-loop.excerpt: LIA never takes critical actions without your consent. Its 6-level HITL system protects you against errors and hallucinations.
human-in-the-loop.body:
Why human validation is essential

Language models can hallucinate or misinterpret intent. LIA solves this by placing humans at the center of every critical decision. No email is sent, no event created, no data modified without your explicit validation.

The 6 approval levels

LIA's HITL system classifies each action into 6 levels:

  • Plan Approval — Before executing a multi-step plan, LIA generates a PlanApprovalRequest containing a plan summary and modifiable parameters, then waits for your go-ahead.
  • Clarification — If intent is ambiguous, LIA asks for details rather than guessing.
  • Draft Critique — For emails or messages, LIA submits a draft for approval before sending.
  • Destructive Confirmation — Any deletion or irreversible modification requires explicit confirmation.
  • FOR_EACH Confirmation — For batch operations, each item can be validated individually.
  • Modifier Review — Parameter changes are presented for verification.

5 possible decisions with confidence

The HITL classifier produces a ClassificationResult with 5 possible decisions, each accompanied by a confidence score between 0.0 and 1.0:

  • APPROVE — The action is validated and passes to the task_orchestrator
  • REJECT — The action is refused, the flow is redirected to the response node
  • EDIT — The user modifies parameters via edited_params, a PlanEditor applies the changes
  • REPLAN — The user reformulates their intent via reformulated_intent, the flow returns to the planner
  • AMBIGUOUS — The system asks a clarification_question to resolve the ambiguity

Native LangGraph interruption

Technically, the approval_gate node uses LangGraph's interrupt() function to suspend graph execution and wait for the user's response. The state is persisted in PostgreSQL, allowing asynchronous resumption even after a disconnection.

You always have the last word

At each validation point, classification strategies are composable: based on tool manifests, estimated cost, data sensitivity, and user role. LIA never bypasses this step.

And that last word is honored to the letter: review loops follow a replay-safe pattern (one interrupt() per node execution, checkpointed loop state — ADR-092), so a resume never replays a past LLM or API call. What you approve, after as many edits as you need, is exactly what gets executed.

Validate once, never twice

A safeguard in the wrong place works against its own intent. Upstream of the plan, a semantic validator could halt on an action it judged "irreversible" — sending an email, booking an appointment, placing a call — while a preview and an explicit confirmation were arriving right after, on exactly the same action. The user had to insist in order to be obeyed.

The rule is now written down: an action that already carries its own confirmation downstream is never halted upstream. The validator judges the structure of the plan — missing parameter, wrong tool, inconsistent cardinality — and not how consequential the action feels. Asking the same question twice adds no safety: it shifts the burden onto the user and eventually teaches them to click without reading.

llm-providers.title: Multi-Provider AI: choose the right model for every task
llm-providers.excerpt: LIA supports many language model providers and lets you configure a different model for each task type: routing, planning, response, agents.
llm-providers.body:
Many providers, one assistant

LIA natively integrates many LLM providers — from proprietary cloud models to locally-run open-source models. Each provider is managed by a dedicated adapter in the LLM factory, and you can add new ones.

56 individually configurable LLM types

LIA defines over 50 LLM types that can be configured separately: router, response, planner, each domain agent, and more. For each type, you can set: provider, model, temperature, top_p, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, max_tokens, timeout and reasoning_effort.

For example:

  • A fast, economical model for routing
  • A powerful model for planning
  • A creative model for responses
  • A local model for privacy

Configuration resolution chain

Each LLM configuration follows a 3-level resolution chain: Admin UI (stored in the database) → Environment variables → Code defaults. An LLMConfigOverrideCache provides O(1) lookups without database queries at runtime. Changes made via the admin interface take immediate effect thanks to cache invalidation.

The multi-provider LLM factory

A single entry point for all providers:

def get_llm(
    llm_type: LLMType,
    config_override: LLMAgentConfig | None = None,
) -> BaseChatModel:
    if config_override is None:
        agent_config = get_llm_config_for_agent(
            settings, llm_type
        )
    else:
        agent_config = config_override

    return ProviderAdapter.create_llm(agent_config)
